It also has real engineering cost - adding a new third-party script (a support widget, an analytics tool, a payment SDK) requires updating the CSP allowlist, which is a common source of "why is this suddenly broken in production" bugs when CSP silently blocks something.
realExample: A payments dashboard sets a strict CSP that only allows scripts from 'self' and https://js.stripe.com (Stripe's hosted payment SDK), and connect-src that explicitly allowlists both the app's own API domain and its WebSocket endpoint (wss://) for real-time order updates - so even if a dependency vulnerability let an attacker inject a malicious script tag, the browser would refuse to execute or connect it anywhere outside that allowlist.
commonMistake: Setting a CSP with 'unsafe-inline' and 'unsafe-eval' broadly just to make errors go away quickly, which defeats most of CSP's actual XSS protection - the safer fix is usually using nonces or hashes for necessary inline scripts, or better, removing inline scripts from the codebase entirely.
interviewAnswer: CSP is a header that restricts what the browser is allowed to load and execute on a page, and it's one of the strongest practical defenses against XSS, because even if an attacker successfully injects a script tag, a tight script-src that only allows 'self' plus specifically trusted domains will make the browser refuse to run it. The real engineering cost is that every third-party integration - an analytics script, a payments SDK, a support widget - needs an explicit CSP allowlist entry, and I've seen teams weaken CSP with 'unsafe-inline' just to unblock something quickly, which quietly removes most of the protection it was providing in the first place.
followUps: What's the difference between CSP's frame-ancestors and the older X-Frame-Options header?
How do nonces work in CSP to allow specific inline scripts safely?
How would you roll out a new, stricter CSP on an existing production app without breaking things?
miniExercise: Write a CSP header for a dashboard that loads its own JS/CSS, embeds a Stripe payment iframe, calls its own API domain, and connects to a WebSocket for live updates - listing the specific directives and values needed, with no wildcards or unsafe-inline.
seniorDiscussion: Your app currently has no CSP and you're tasked with rolling one out on a mature production codebase with many legacy inline scripts and several third-party integrations. Do you go straight to enforce mode, or start with Content-Security-Policy-Report-Only to gather violation reports first - and how do you use that reporting data to build the final policy without a long, risky trial-and-error cycle directly in production?

title: Auth vs Authz, XSS, CSRF & Same-Origin Policy
explanation: Authentication (who are you - login) and authorization (what are you allowed to do - RBAC/permissions) are distinct concerns that are often conflated; frontend route guards for either are a UX convenience only, never a real security boundary - the backend must independently enforce both on every request, since any frontend check can be bypassed by calling the API directly. XSS (executing attacker-controlled script in your page, e.g. via unsanitized user input rendered as HTML) and CSRF (tricking a logged-in user's browser into making an unwanted request to your site using their existing session) are the two classic web attacks the same-origin policy and modern defenses (CSP, SameSite cookies, CSRF tokens) exist to mitigate.
whyItMatters: This is the single most important distinction in frontend security interviews: candidates who say "we hide the admin button if the user isn't an admin, so it's secure" are describing a UX nicety, not access control - the real enforcement must happen server-side on every protected endpoint, using the authenticated session/token to check permissions, independent of anything the client claims or hides. Getting this wrong in a real product (RBAC-gated features, admin panels, payment authorization) is a direct security vulnerability, not a style preference.
realExample: A support dashboard hides the "Refund Payment" button in the UI for non-admin roles (good UX, reduces clutter and mistakes), but the actual POST /api/payments/:id/refund endpoint independently checks the authenticated user's role server-side before processing the refund - so even if someone opens devtools, finds the API endpoint, and calls it directly with a non-admin session, the backend rejects it regardless of what the frontend chose to render.
commonMistake: Believing that hiding a button, disabling a route, or checking a role in frontend JS is a security control - it is purely a UX convenience, and any determined user (or attacker) can call the underlying API directly, bypassing every frontend check entirely, so real authorization must always be enforced server-side.
interviewAnswer: Authentication proves who you are, authorization decides what you're allowed to do once you're known, and the critical thing I always emphasize is that frontend checks for either - hiding an admin button, redirecting away from a protected route - are purely UX, never real security, because anyone can call the API directly and skip the frontend entirely. On XSS and CSRF: XSS is getting a malicious script to execute in your page, usually through unsanitized user input rendered as HTML, and CSRF is tricking a user's browser into firing a request to your site using their already-logged-in session, typically from another tab or a malicious page. Defenses like CSP, escaping/sanitizing output, SameSite cookies, and CSRF tokens all exist because the same-origin policy alone doesn't fully close these gaps.
followUps: Why doesn't the same-origin policy alone prevent CSRF?
How does a SameSite=Strict or Lax cookie attribute mitigate CSRF?
Give an example of a real XSS vector in a React app despite React's default escaping.
miniExercise: Given a mock RBAC dashboard where the frontend hides an "Approve Refund" button for non-admins, write out (in words or pseudocode) exactly what backend checks must independently exist for the refund endpoint to be genuinely secure, regardless of what the frontend renders.
seniorDiscussion: Your app moves from localStorage-based JWT auth to httpOnly cookie-based sessions to reduce XSS token-theft risk, but this reintroduces CSRF risk since cookies are sent automatically by the browser. What's your full mitigation strategy - SameSite attribute choice, CSRF tokens, double-submit cookies, checking custom request headers - and what are the trade-offs for a SPA that also needs to support a separate mobile app hitting the same API?

title: Cookies, Sessions & Storage Strategy
explanation: A session is server-side state (who's logged in, what they can do) that needs to be linked to each request somehow - traditionally via a cookie holding a session ID, or in a token-based (JWT) approach, via a bearer token sent in an Authorization header or stored in a cookie. Key cookie attributes - HttpOnly (invisible to JS), Secure (HTTPS only), SameSite (Strict/Lax/None, controls cross-site sending) - directly determine your app's exposure to XSS-based token theft and CSRF.
whyItMatters: Choosing a session strategy (stateful server sessions vs stateless JWTs, cookie vs header-based tokens) has real consequences for logout-everywhere behavior, horizontal scaling (stateless JWTs don't need a shared session store, but can't be revoked instantly without extra infrastructure like a blocklist), and security posture - this is a common systems-design-adjacent frontend/full-stack interview topic.
realExample: An app uses short-lived JWT access tokens (15 minutes) in httpOnly cookies for API auth, plus a separate longer-lived refresh token (also httpOnly, SameSite=Strict) used only against a dedicated /refresh endpoint - this limits the blast radius if an access token were ever somehow leaked, while avoiding the need for a shared server-side session store, which matters for horizontally scaling the API across multiple stateless instances.
commonMistake: Choosing stateless JWTs for a feature that specifically needs instant, guaranteed revocation (like "log out this device remotely" or "immediately revoke access after an admin disables a user") without also building a token blocklist or short-enough expiry - a plain stateless JWT can't be un-issued once handed out, only expire on its own schedule.
interviewAnswer: A session just needs some way to link a request back to server-side state about who's logged in - classically a cookie holding a session ID that the server looks up in a store, or more recently a token like a JWT that encodes claims directly so the server doesn't need a lookup at all. The trade-off is that stateless JWTs scale easily since there's no shared session store, but they're hard to revoke instantly - you either wait for expiry or maintain a blocklist, which brings back some server-side state anyway. Whatever the strategy, I'd keep the actual token in an httpOnly, Secure cookie with an appropriate SameSite value rather than somewhere JS can read it, to limit XSS-based theft.
followUps: Why can't you instantly revoke a stateless JWT the way you can a server-side session?
What's the practical difference between SameSite=Strict and SameSite=Lax for a login cookie?
How would you implement 'log out of all devices' with JWT-based auth?
miniExercise: Design (in words) a token strategy for an app that needs both good horizontal scalability and the ability to instantly revoke a compromised user's access within seconds - explain what you'd sacrifice and what infrastructure (if any) you'd add.
seniorDiscussion: Your product needs to support both a web app (cookies work fine) and a mobile app (cookies are awkward) sharing the same backend auth system. Do you standardize on Authorization-header bearer tokens for both, use cookies for web and headers for mobile with a shared token-issuing backend, or maintain two separate auth flows - and how do you keep CSRF/XSS protections consistent across both?

title: Caching & CDNs
explanation: HTTP caching is controlled mainly by Cache-Control (max-age, no-store, no-cache, must-revalidate, immutable) plus validators like ETag/Last-Modified for conditional requests (304 Not Modified). CDNs cache static assets (and sometimes API responses) at edge locations physically closer to users, and cache-busting via content-hashed filenames (app.a1b2c3.js) lets you set extremely long cache lifetimes safely, since a new deploy produces a new filename rather than requiring cache invalidation.
whyItMatters: Correct caching is one of the highest-leverage performance levers available - a well-cached static asset (JS/CSS/images/fonts) served from a nearby CDN edge can load in single-digit milliseconds versus hundreds for an uncached origin request - but it's also a common source of "why are users still seeing the old version after we deployed" bugs when cache headers or invalidation are misconfigured, which is especially dangerous for something like stale pricing information.
simpleExample:
Cache-Control: public, max-age=31536000, immutable  // hashed static asset, cache "forever"
Cache-Control: no-store                              // never cache: sensitive API responses (e.g. account balance)
Cache-Control: private, max-age=0, must-revalidate     // always revalidate with the server before using cache
realExample: A dashboard's JS/CSS bundles are named with content hashes (main.9f8e7d.js) and served with Cache-Control: max-age=31536000, immutable from a CDN, so browsers cache them essentially forever and only refetch when a new deploy changes the hash (and thus the filename) - while the API response for the user's live account balance is served with Cache-Control: no-store, ensuring it's never accidentally shown stale after a payment.
commonMistake: Setting a long max-age on an API response or HTML page that contains dynamic or sensitive data (account balance, permission-gated content), causing users to see stale or even incorrect data until the cache naturally expires - versioned/hashed static assets are safe to cache aggressively, but the dynamic responses that reference them usually shouldn't be.
interviewAnswer: For static assets I want extremely aggressive caching - a long max-age plus immutable - but that's only safe because the filename is content-hashed, so a new deploy is a genuinely new URL rather than requiring anyone to invalidate a cache. For anything dynamic or sensitive, like an account balance or permission-gated data, I'd use no-store or a short max-age with must-revalidate so the browser always checks with the server rather than risking stale data. A CDN sits in front of all of this and serves cached static content from an edge location near the user, which cuts latency dramatically compared to hitting the origin server for every request.
followUps: What's the difference between Cache-Control: no-cache and no-store?
How does an ETag-based conditional request (304 Not Modified) save bandwidth compared to max-age alone?
How do you handle cache invalidation for an HTML page itself, which usually can't be content-hashed in its URL?
miniExercise: For a product page, decide appropriate Cache-Control values for: the HTML document itself, a content-hashed JS bundle, a user's live shopping cart API response, and a rarely-changing list of country codes - and justify each choice.
seniorDiscussion: Your team just shipped a critical pricing bug fix, but some users are still seeing the old (wrong) price for up to an hour after deploy because of aggressive CDN caching on an API response. How do you both fix this incident quickly (cache purge/invalidation) and redesign the caching strategy so a future pricing bug fix propagates immediately without sacrificing the performance benefits of caching in general?

title: Core Web Vitals
explanation: Core Web Vitals are Google's standardized UX metrics: LCP (Largest Contentful Paint - how fast the main content renders, target under 2.5s), INP (Interaction to Next Paint, replacing FID - how responsive the page feels to real interactions, target under 200ms), and CLS (Cumulative Layout Shift - how much visible content jumps around unexpectedly, target under 0.1). They're measured from real user data (field data, via Chrome UX Report) as well as lab tools (Lighthouse), and they factor directly into Google search ranking.
whyItMatters: These metrics are a shared, concrete vocabulary for "is the app fast" that product, engineering, and even SEO/marketing teams can all reference, replacing vague complaints like "the site feels slow." Optimizing them requires understanding their specific causes: LCP is often a slow hero image or render-blocking resource, CLS is usually images/ads/fonts loading without reserved space, and INP is often heavy JS blocking the main thread during a click or input.
realExample: A checkout page's LCP is dominated by a large hero product image that loads late; adding fetchpriority="high" (or Next.js's Image priority prop) and preloading it moves LCP from 4.2s to 1.8s, while a previously janky "apply coupon" button that froze the UI for 400ms on click gets its heavy synchronous discount-calculation logic moved to run in chunks or a Web Worker, improving INP well under the 200ms target.
commonMistake: Optimizing only in a lab environment (Lighthouse scores in local dev, on a fast machine and network) and declaring victory, without checking real-user field data (Chrome UX Report / your own RUM), which often tells a very different story once you account for actual user devices, network conditions, and geographic latency.
interviewAnswer: Core Web Vitals give me three concrete, standardized numbers to reason about perceived performance: LCP for how fast the main content shows up, INP for how responsive the page feels when someone actually interacts with it, and CLS for how much things unexpectedly jump around. In practice, LCP problems are usually a slow-loading hero image or a render-blocking resource, CLS problems are almost always images, ads, or web fonts loading without reserved space, and INP problems are heavy JS blocking the main thread right when someone clicks or types. I always check real user field data, not just a Lighthouse lab score, because lab conditions rarely match what actual users experience on their devices and networks.
followUps: What's the difference between lab data (Lighthouse) and field data (CrUX) for Core Web Vitals, and why might they disagree?
How would you debug a high CLS score on a page that looks visually stable to you locally?
Why did Google replace FID with INP as a Core Web Vital?
miniExercise: Run Lighthouse on a real page you have access to, identify the single biggest contributor to its LCP or CLS score, and propose one concrete fix (with the specific attribute or technique) for it.
seniorDiscussion: Your marketing team wants to add three new third-party scripts (a chat widget, a heatmap tool, and an A/B testing library) to a page whose Core Web Vitals are already borderline. How do you evaluate the real performance cost of each one before approving it, and what technical guardrails (loading strategy, budget alerts in CI, a performance budget in your build pipeline) would you put in place to prevent silent regressions going forward?

title: Scope & Variables (var, let, const)
explanation: var is function-scoped and hoisted with an initial value of undefined, while let and const are block-scoped and live in the Temporal Dead Zone until their declaration line executes. const prevents reassignment of the binding itself, not mutation of the value it points to - a const array or object can still have its contents changed. Understanding scope correctly explains classic bugs like a var-based loop variable being shared across all closures created inside it.
whyItMatters: Scope bugs are among the most common source of subtle, hard-to-reproduce issues, especially in loops that create closures (event handlers, setTimeout callbacks, array callbacks capturing a loop variable). Modern codebases use let/const almost exclusively for exactly this reason - block scoping matches how engineers actually reason about variable lifetimes.
realExample: A table component that attaches a click handler per row inside a for loop using var accidentally has every row's handler reference the same final value of the loop variable (e.g. always the last row's ID), causing every row click to act on the wrong row - switching the loop to let fixes it immediately because each iteration gets its own binding, which is exactly what the closure captures.
commonMistake: Using var out of habit (often from older JS or copy-pasted code) inside a loop that creates closures, then being confused why every callback references the same final value instead of the value at the time the closure was created.
interviewAnswer: var is function-scoped and gets hoisted with an undefined placeholder, while let and const are block-scoped and stay in a Temporal Dead Zone until the line they're declared on actually runs, which is why referencing them earlier throws instead of silently giving undefined. const only locks the binding, not the value - I can still push into a const array or mutate a const object's properties, just not reassign the variable itself. The classic interview gotcha is a var inside a for loop combined with setTimeout or an event handler - because var is shared across iterations, every callback ends up referencing the same final value, which let fixes by giving each iteration its own scoped binding.
followUps: What is the Temporal Dead Zone and why does it exist?
Why does const not make an object or array immutable?
How would you make an object's properties truly immutable in JS?
miniExercise: Predict and explain the output of a for loop using var with three setTimeout calls logging the loop variable, versus the same loop using let - then verify in a JS console.
seniorDiscussion: Your team has a lint rule banning var entirely. Are there any legitimate remaining use cases for var in modern JS/TS codebases (e.g. certain hoisting-dependent patterns, or older browser support constraints), or is a hard ban always correct for a modern React/Next.js/TypeScript project?

title: Type Coercion & Equality
explanation: JS coerces types implicitly in many operations - == triggers type coercion before comparing (e.g. "5" == 5 is true, null == undefined is true, but null == 0 is false due to specific coercion rules), while === compares both type and value with no coercion. Truthy/falsy rules (0, "", null, undefined, NaN, false are falsy; everything else, including "0" and [] and {}, is truthy) drive conditional logic throughout JS and trip up engineers coming from stricter languages.
whyItMatters: Relying on == or on truthy/falsy shortcuts without understanding their exact rules is a common source of subtle bugs - e.g. checking if (value) to test "is this field filled in" silently treats a valid input of 0 or an empty string differently than intended, which matters directly in form validation (a numeric field where 0 is a valid value) and API response handling (an empty array [] being truthy even though it represents "no results").
simpleExample:
0 == "0"       // true  (coercion)
0 == ""         // true  (coercion)
"" == "0"       // false (coercion rules differ pairwise)
[] == false     // true  (coercion chain: [] -> "" -> 0)
Number("") === 0 // true, but "" is falsy while 0 is also falsy - different reasons
realExample: A quantity input field in an order form uses if (quantity) to check "was a value entered," which silently breaks for a legitimate quantity of 0 (treated as falsy, so the form thinks the field is empty) - the correct check is if (quantity !== undefined && quantity !== null && quantity !== "") or converting explicitly and checking Number.isNaN, since 0 is a meaningful, valid value here, not an absence of one.
commonMistake: Using if (value) as a shorthand for "is this present/valid" when 0, empty string, or an empty array are all legitimate values in the domain (a discount amount, an optional text field, an empty-but-successful search result) - falsy does not mean invalid or absent, and conflating them causes real product bugs.
interviewAnswer: == coerces types before comparing, which leads to surprising results like "5" == 5 being true or null == undefined being true, while === never coerces and compares type and value directly - so I default to === everywhere and only reach for == in the rare, well-understood case like checking value == null to catch both null and undefined at once. On truthy/falsy, the rule is simple - 0, empty string, null, undefined, NaN, and false are falsy, everything else is truthy - but that trips people up constantly in real forms, because 0 is a falsy value that's often a perfectly valid input, so if (quantity) is a bug waiting to happen for a quantity field that can legitimately be zero.
followUps: Why does [] == false evaluate to true?
What's a legitimate, intentional use case for == instead of ===?
How does Object.is differ from === for edge cases like NaN and -0?
miniExercise: Write a function isEmpty(value) that correctly distinguishes between 0, false, an empty string, null, undefined, and an empty array/object - deciding intentionally which of these count as "empty" for a generic form-field validator, and explain your reasoning for each.
seniorDiscussion: Your codebase has a mix of == and === used inconsistently across years of contributions. Would you write a lint rule to ban == entirely, or are there specific, well-scoped exceptions worth allowing (like value == null) - and how do you roll out that lint rule without a disruptive mass-refactor PR?

title: Functions, Closures, Hoisting & TDZ
explanation: A closure is a function that retains access to variables from its enclosing scope even after that outer function has returned - this is the mechanism behind private state, memoization caches, and event handler factories. Function declarations are fully hoisted (usable before their definition line), function expressions and arrow functions are not (only the variable binding is hoisted, per var/let/const rules), and the Temporal Dead Zone applies to let/const-declared functions referenced before their line runs.
whyItMatters: Closures are the foundation of most non-trivial JS patterns: React hooks (useState's setter closing over the current render's state), debounce/throttle utilities, memoization caches, and module-pattern private variables all depend on understanding exactly what a closure captures and when. Misunderstanding this is the direct cause of the extremely common "stale closure" bug in React (a callback captures an old state value from a previous render).
realExample: A debounced search-input handler is created once with useMemo/useCallback and closes over the current onSearch callback prop; if the closure captures a stale version of onSearch from an earlier render (because it wasn't included in a dependency array), typing in the search box calls an outdated version of the search function - a textbook stale-closure bug that closures explain precisely.
commonMistake: Assuming a closure "copies" the value of a captured variable at creation time, when it actually captures a live reference to the variable itself - so if the outer variable changes later, the closure sees the updated value, not a snapshot, which is exactly what causes many React stale-closure and loop-related bugs.
interviewAnswer: A closure means an inner function keeps access to its outer function's variables even after the outer function has already returned, because it holds a live reference to that scope, not a copied snapshot. This is what makes patterns like a counter with private state, or a memoization cache, possible without any global variables. It's also directly responsible for a very common React bug - a stale closure - where a callback or effect captures an old value of a prop or state variable from a previous render because the closure was created before that value updated, and the dependency array didn't include it.
followUps: What exactly does a closure capture - the value or the variable binding?
Why are function declarations hoisted differently from function expressions?
How would you use a closure to implement a simple memoization cache from scratch?
miniExercise: Write a function createRateLimiter(maxCalls) that returns a function which allows only maxCalls invocations, using a closure to track call count privately, with no external/global state.
seniorDiscussion: In a large React codebase, stale closures inside useEffect and useCallback are a recurring source of hard-to-reproduce bugs (especially with WebSocket handlers or debounced functions). What's your team's strategy for catching these systematically - the exhaustive-deps ESLint rule, code review heuristics, or architectural patterns (like refs for "latest value" access) that sidestep the problem entirely?

title: this, call, apply & bind
explanation: this is determined by how a function is called, not where it's defined: as a method (obj.method()) it's the object before the dot, as a plain function call it's undefined in strict mode (or the global object otherwise), as a constructor (new Fn()) it's the new instance, and arrow functions don't have their own this - they inherit it lexically from the enclosing scope at definition time. call/apply invoke a function immediately with an explicit this (apply takes arguments as an array), while bind returns a new function permanently bound to a given this.
whyItMatters: this-related bugs are extremely common when passing a method as a callback (e.g. class method as an event handler, or object method passed to setTimeout/array methods) without preserving its binding - the method executes with the wrong this and silently returns undefined for what should be an object property. Arrow functions solve most of this in modern code by inheriting this lexically, which is exactly why class fields defined as arrow functions became a popular pattern for React class components before hooks.
realExample: A class-based WebSocket connection manager has a handleMessage(event) method that needs to update this.state when a message arrives; passing socket.onmessage = this.handleMessage directly loses the this binding, so the method fails silently trying to access this.state - the fix is either socket.onmessage = this.handleMessage.bind(this) in the constructor, or defining handleMessage as an arrow function class field, which lexically captures this from the class instance automatically.
commonMistake: Passing an object method as a callback (to an event listener, setTimeout, or array method) without binding it first, then being confused why this inside the method is undefined or refers to the wrong object - the method 'remembers' its code but not its intended this, which is only determined at call time.
interviewAnswer: this is decided by how a function gets called, not by where it's written - call it as obj.method() and this is obj, call it as a detached function and this is undefined in strict mode, use new and this is the new instance being constructed. call and apply let me invoke a function immediately with an explicit this - the only difference is apply takes arguments as an array - while bind returns a brand new function permanently locked to a given this, which I'd use when passing a method somewhere as a callback, like an event listener. Arrow functions sidestep this whole problem for most modern code because they don't have their own this at all - they just inherit it lexically from wherever they were defined, which is why they're the default choice for callbacks inside class methods or React components.
followUps: Why don't arrow functions have their own this, and what do they use instead?
What does 'this' refer to inside a regular function called without any object context, in strict mode versus non-strict mode?
How would you rewrite a class method to avoid needing .bind(this) in the constructor?
miniExercise: Given a class with a regular (non-arrow) method that's passed directly as an event handler and breaks because of a lost this binding, fix it three different ways: .bind() in the constructor, an arrow function class field, and wrapping it in an inline arrow function at the call site.
seniorDiscussion: Your codebase has a mix of class components (with manually bound methods) and function components with hooks. If you're migrating the class components to hooks, what this-binding issues do you expect to simply disappear, and are there any behavioral differences (e.g. around stale values in callbacks) that the migration could introduce if done carelessly?

title: Objects, Prototypes & Classes
explanation: Every JS object has an internal prototype link (accessible via Object.getPrototypeOf or the deprecated __proto__) forming a prototype chain that property lookups walk up if a property isn't found directly on the object. class syntax is largely sugar over this same prototype-based system - methods defined in a class body live on the prototype (shared across instances), while fields assigned in the constructor (or as class fields) live on each instance directly. Understanding this explains why methods are shared (memory-efficient) while instance data isn't.
whyItMatters: Most engineers use class syntax daily without needing the prototype chain details, but it resurfaces in real debugging: understanding why Object.keys(instance) doesn't include prototype methods, why hasOwnProperty matters when iterating an object with for...in, or why extending a built-in like Error requires care (instanceof checks after transpilation) all trace back to prototypes.
realExample: A custom PaymentError class extends the built-in Error to carry a structured error code (e.g. card_declined, insufficient_funds) for consistent handling across a payment flow; because class extends Error relies on the prototype chain, error.name, error.stack, and instanceof PaymentError all need to be verified after any build/transpilation step, since older TypeScript targets historically broke instanceof checks for classes extending built-ins.
commonMistake: Assuming class fields assigned in the constructor are shared across instances the way methods are - they're not; each instance gets its own copy of constructor-assigned data, while only methods defined in the class body (or object literal via prototype) are actually shared via the prototype chain, which is why mutating one instance's data never affects another's.
interviewAnswer: Every object in JS has a hidden link to a prototype object, and when you access a property, JS walks up that chain until it finds it or hits null - class syntax is essentially sugar on top of this same system, where methods you define in the class body end up on the prototype and are shared across every instance, while anything you assign with this.x in the constructor lives directly on that specific instance. That's a useful mental model for memory - a hundred instances of a class share one copy of each method, but each carries its own instance data - and it explains real gotchas like why extending a built-in class such as Error needs extra care with instanceof checks depending on your build target.
followUps: What's the difference between Object.create(proto) and using the class/new syntax?
Why might instanceof give an unexpected result after certain TypeScript/Babel transpilation targets?
How would you implement private instance fields in a class, and how does that differ from just a naming convention like _field?
miniExercise: Create a class CustomApiError extending Error that adds a statusCode and code property, and verify with instanceof that both instanceof CustomApiError and instanceof Error work correctly after being thrown and caught.
seniorDiscussion: Your team is deciding between class-based data models (with methods) versus plain objects/interfaces plus standalone utility functions for domain logic (e.g. an Invoice model). What are the real trade-offs for testability, serialization (e.g. over a WebSocket or API response), and structural typing in TypeScript, and which would you default to for a typical dashboard's domain layer?

title: Arrays, Map/Set, Destructuring & Spread/Rest
explanation: Arrays have a rich set of higher-order methods (map, filter, reduce, find, some, every) that should generally be preferred over manual for loops for clarity, plus Map (ordered key-value pairs with any key type, unlike plain objects limited to string/symbol keys) and Set (unique value collections) for specific use cases. Destructuring extracts values from arrays/objects into variables concisely, while spread (...) expands an iterable/object into individual elements/properties and rest (...) collects remaining elements into an array/object - visually identical syntax with opposite purposes depending on context.
whyItMatters: Real data-heavy UI (a table of orders, deduplicating a list of user IDs, merging default and user-provided settings objects) leans on these constantly - reduce for building lookup maps or totals, Set for deduplication, destructuring plus default values for cleanly handling optional API response fields, and spread for immutable state updates in React (returning a new array/object instead of mutating).
simpleExample:
const { name, email, role = "viewer" } = user; // destructuring + default
const uniqueIds = [...new Set(orders.map(o => o.userId))]; // dedupe via Set
const updated = { ...invoice, status: "paid" }; // immutable update via spread
const [first, ...rest] = items; // rest collects remaining elements
realExample: A table showing orders grouped by customer builds a Map<customerId, Order[]> using reduce, since Map preserves insertion order and allows non-string keys cleanly; updating a single order's status in React state uses orders.map(o => o.id === id ? { ...o, status: "shipped" } : o) - spreading to create a new object instead of mutating the original, which is required for React to detect the change via reference comparison.
commonMistake: Mutating an array or object directly (push, splice, direct property assignment) inside React state instead of creating a new reference via spread or map/filter - React's change detection relies on reference equality, so a mutated-but-same-reference array won't trigger a re-render, causing a UI that silently doesn't update.
interviewAnswer: For collections I default to array methods like map, filter, and reduce over manual loops because they read closer to intent and avoid a whole class of off-by-one bugs. Map and Set solve specific gaps in plain objects - Map allows any key type and keeps insertion order reliably, Set gives me deduplication essentially for free. Destructuring and spread/rest look like the same ... syntax but do opposite things depending on which side of an assignment they're on - spread expands a collection into individual items, rest gathers individual items back into a collection - and I use spread constantly in React specifically to create new object/array references instead of mutating, since that's what React's change detection depends on.
followUps: When would you reach for reduce over a chain of map and filter, and what's the trade-off?
Why does React state require a new array/object reference instead of an in-place mutation?
What's a practical use case for Map over a plain object as a key-value store?
miniExercise: Given an array of order objects with a status field, write a one-liner using reduce (or Map) that groups them into an object keyed by status, each value being the array of matching orders.
seniorDiscussion: Your team debates whether to standardize on Immer (or a similar immutability helper) for complex nested state updates versus writing manual spread-based immutable updates everywhere. For a dashboard with deeply nested filter/sort/pagination state, what's your take on the trade-off between Immer's ergonomics and the "hidden mutation" learning curve it introduces for new team members?

title: Immutability & Higher-Order Functions
explanation: Immutability means not mutating existing data structures in place, instead producing new ones with the desired changes - this makes state changes predictable, easy to diff (reference equality checks become meaningful), and safe to share across parts of an app without unexpected side effects. A higher-order function either takes a function as an argument, returns a function, or both - map/filter/reduce, debounce/throttle wrappers, and React hooks that return handlers are all higher-order functions in practice.
whyItMatters: React's whole rendering model leans on immutability - useMemo, React.memo, and dependency arrays all use reference equality (Object.is) to decide whether something changed, so mutating state directly can cause React to miss an update entirely (no re-render) even though the data technically changed. Higher-order functions are also the backbone of most reusable logic - a generic withRetry(fn) wrapper, a debounce(fn, delay) utility, or a createApiClient(config) factory are all patterns senior engineers reach for to avoid duplicating logic.
realExample: A notifications panel's "mark all as read" action returns a brand new array of new notification objects (via map + spread) rather than mutating the existing array in place, so React.memo on individual notification items and the parent list's re-render logic both correctly detect exactly which items changed via reference comparison, instead of either missing the update or re-rendering everything unnecessarily.
commonMistake: Mutating a nested object or array directly (e.g. notifications[0].read = true) and then calling setState with the same outer array reference, expecting React to detect the change - React sees the same array reference and may skip re-rendering entirely, since it doesn't deep-compare state by default.
interviewAnswer: Immutability means I never change an existing array or object in place - I create a new one with the change applied - which matters enormously in React because so much of its optimization (memo, useMemo, dependency arrays) relies on cheap reference equality checks rather than expensive deep comparison. Higher-order functions are just functions that take or return other functions, and I use them constantly for cross-cutting concerns - a generic retry wrapper around an API call, a debounce utility, or a factory that returns a configured API client - because they let me add behavior around a function without duplicating that behavior everywhere it's used.
followUps: Why does React.memo sometimes fail to prevent a re-render even though 'nothing visibly changed'?
What's the performance cost of always creating new objects/arrays for immutable updates, and when does it start to matter?
Write a higher-order function that adds console-based timing/logging around any function without modifying its original code.
miniExercise: Refactor a function that mutates an array in place (e.g. sorting or filtering with side effects on the original array) to instead return a new array immutably, and explain what React bug this refactor would prevent if that array were component state.
seniorDiscussion: For very large, deeply nested state (a complex form or a big normalized data cache), manual spread-based immutable updates become verbose and error-prone. Would you introduce Immer, restructure the state to be flatter (normalized, similar to a database), or use a state management library that handles this - and how do you weigh the added dependency/learning-curve cost against the ergonomic win for a team of varying experience levels?

title: Recursion
explanation: Recursion is a function calling itself on a smaller version of the problem, with a base case that stops the recursion - useful for naturally tree-shaped or nested data (a comments thread, a nested category/permission tree, folder structures) where an iterative solution would need a manual stack. JS doesn't (reliably) support tail-call optimization in most engines, so deep recursion (thousands of levels) can hit a "Maximum call stack size exceeded" error, which is a real practical constraint, not just a theoretical one.
whyItMatters: Nested/tree-shaped data shows up constantly in real products - a permissions tree for RBAC (roles containing sub-roles or nested permission groups), a comment thread with replies-to-replies, a category hierarchy for a product catalog - and recursion is usually the clearest way to traverse or transform these structures, though depth limits mean very deep or user-controlled-depth trees need either an iterative approach or an explicit depth guard.
realExample: An RBAC settings page renders a nested permissions tree (roles that can contain sub-roles, each with their own permissions) using a recursive PermissionNode component that renders itself for each child - clean and directly mirrors the tree's actual shape, though the team adds a maxDepth guard since role nesting is admin-configurable and an accidental or malicious deeply-nested structure could otherwise blow the call stack or freeze the UI.
commonMistake: Writing unbounded recursion over data whose depth isn't fully controlled by the codebase (like a user-editable comment thread or an admin-configurable permission tree) without a depth limit or a stack-safe iterative fallback, risking a stack overflow in production on unusually deep real-world data.
interviewAnswer: Recursion is when a function calls itself on a smaller piece of the same problem until it hits a base case that stops it, and it's the natural tool for genuinely tree-shaped data, like a nested comments thread or a permissions hierarchy, where the recursive code ends up mirroring the actual shape of the data. The practical catch in JS is that most engines don't reliably optimize tail calls, so very deep recursion - thousands of levels - can actually overflow the call stack, which is a real concern if the data's depth isn't fully controlled by your own code, like a user-generated comment thread; in that case I'd either cap the depth explicitly or fall back to an iterative approach with an explicit stack.
followUps: Why doesn't JS reliably support tail-call optimization even though the spec allows it?
How would you convert a recursive function into an iterative one using an explicit stack?
What's a real risk of using recursion on user-controlled-depth data, like a comment thread?
miniExercise: Write a recursive function countNodes(tree) that counts all nodes in a nested permissions tree (each node has a children array), then add a depth guard that throws a clear error if the tree exceeds a maximum depth of 50.
seniorDiscussion: Your app renders a deeply nested, user-editable folder structure (like a file manager) that occasionally causes a stack overflow for a small number of power users with very deep folder trees. Do you cap nesting depth at the product level (simpler, but a UX restriction), rewrite the traversal iteratively with an explicit stack (more code, no UX change), or virtualize/lazy-render deep branches so only visible depth is ever processed at once?

title: Currying & Memoization
explanation: Currying transforms a function taking multiple arguments into a sequence of functions each taking one argument (or a subset), enabling partial application - useful for creating specialized versions of a general function (e.g. a generic validator curried into field-specific validators). Memoization caches a function's return value keyed by its arguments, trading memory for avoiding redundant expensive computation - useMemo in React is a memoization mechanism scoped to a component's render lifecycle.
whyItMatters: Currying shows up in real code as configuration-then-execution patterns - a curried createValidator(rules)(value) lets you build a reusable, pre-configured validator function once and reuse it across many form fields. Memoization is directly relevant to React performance work (useMemo, useCallback, React.memo) and to avoiding redundant expensive computations like re-sorting or re-filtering a large dataset on every render when the inputs haven't actually changed.
realExample: A form-validation library curries its rule functions (minLength(8), matchesPattern(regex)) so each field in a large onboarding form gets a pre-configured, reusable validator without recreating the same logic per field, while an expensive client-side "compute portfolio risk score" calculation is wrapped in a memoized function keyed by the current holdings array reference, so re-rendering the dashboard for an unrelated UI change (like opening a settings modal) doesn't recompute the same expensive result.
commonMistake: Memoizing a function using an argument-based cache key without considering cache growth or argument identity - e.g. caching by JSON.stringify(args) for large or frequently-changing objects can be slow to hash and can leak memory unboundedly if the cache is never cleared, especially for a long-lived dashboard session that calls the function with thousands of distinct argument combinations over time.
interviewAnswer: Currying breaks a multi-argument function into a chain of single-argument functions, so you can partially apply it - for example building a reusable, pre-configured validator once from a generic rule function, then just supplying the value later on each field. Memoization is about caching a function's result keyed by its arguments so repeated calls with the same inputs skip recomputation - useMemo in React is essentially a scoped version of this, tied to a component's render and its dependency array. The trade-off with memoization is always memory versus speed, and for anything with unbounded or high-cardinality inputs, you need a cache eviction strategy or you risk trading a CPU problem for a memory leak.
followUps: What's the difference between currying and simple partial application?
How would you decide whether a given useMemo call is actually worth its overhead?
What cache eviction strategy would you use for a memoization cache that could otherwise grow unboundedly?
miniExercise: Write a curried function createDiscountRule(minAmount)(discountPercent)(orderTotal) that returns whether a discount applies and at what rate, then create two specialized discount rules from it for different minimum order amounts.
seniorDiscussion: Your team wants to memoize an expensive, pure data-transformation function used across several dashboard widgets, but its inputs are large objects (not primitives) that change reference on every parent re-render even when their content is the same. Do you deep-compare inputs before checking the cache (slower per-call, but better hit rate), rely on stable references upstream (requires other refactors), or decide memoization isn't worth it here - how do you make that call?

title: Debounce & Throttle
explanation: Debounce delays invoking a function until a burst of calls has paused for a specified time (each new call resets the timer) - ideal for "wait until the user stops typing" scenarios like search-as-you-type. Throttle guarantees a function runs at most once per specified interval regardless of how many times it's called - ideal for high-frequency events like scroll or resize/mousemove where you still want periodic updates during continuous activity, not just after it stops.
whyItMatters: A search input that fires an API call on every keystroke without debouncing can generate dozens of wasted requests per search term and race conditions where an earlier request's response arrives after a later one's (showing stale results); a scroll-position handler that runs unthrottled can run hundreds of times per second and tank frame rate. Choosing correctly between them - and implementing cancellation for the in-flight request in a debounced search - is a very common real interview and real production concern.
realExample: A search-as-you-type box debounces the API call by 300ms so it only fires once the user pauses typing, and additionally cancels any in-flight request (via AbortController) when a new one starts, to avoid a slower earlier response overwriting the correct, more recent results; a live-updating "scroll to load more" infinite-scroll table throttles its scroll handler to run at most every 200ms, so it still responds promptly during continuous scrolling without checking scroll position on every single scroll event.
commonMistake: Using debounce for a scroll or resize handler that needs periodic feedback during continuous activity (debounce would only fire after scrolling stops entirely, feeling unresponsive), or using throttle for a search input (which would still fire many unnecessary intermediate requests while the user is actively typing) - picking the wrong one for the interaction pattern produces a subtly broken UX.
interviewAnswer: Debounce waits for a pause - every new call resets the timer, so the function only runs once activity has actually stopped, which is exactly right for a search box where I want to wait until the user stops typing before firing a request. Throttle instead guarantees the function runs at most once every fixed interval no matter how often it's called, which fits something like a scroll handler where I want periodic updates the whole time the user is scrolling, not just a single update at the very end. Picking the wrong one is a common subtle UX bug - debouncing a scroll handler makes it feel unresponsive during the scroll, and throttling a search box still fires more requests than necessary while typing.
followUps: How would you cancel a debounced search's in-flight API request when a newer keystroke supersedes it?
What's the difference between leading-edge and trailing-edge throttle/debounce?
How do libraries like lodash implement debounce/throttle differently from a hand-rolled version, and what edge cases do they handle?
miniExercise: Implement a debounce(fn, delay) function from scratch (no libraries) and use it to wrap a mock search function, verifying that rapid successive calls only result in one final invocation after the delay.
seniorDiscussion: Your search-as-you-type feature is debounced at 300ms, but users on slower connections still occasionally see results from an earlier, slower-resolving request overwrite the correct results from a later, faster one. Debouncing alone doesn't fix this race condition - what's the full solution (request cancellation via AbortController, request sequence numbers/tokens, or something else), and how would you test it reliably given it's a timing-dependent bug?

title: Promises, async/await & Combinators
explanation: A Promise represents an eventual value from an async operation, in one of three states (pending, fulfilled, rejected); async/await is syntax sugar that makes Promise-based code read like synchronous code, with try/catch for error handling. The Promise combinators handle different multi-async needs: Promise.all rejects as soon as any promise rejects (fails fast, good for "all must succeed"), Promise.allSettled waits for every promise regardless of outcome (good for "run all, tell me what happened to each"), Promise.race resolves/rejects with whichever settles first, and Promise.any resolves with the first success, ignoring rejections unless all reject.
whyItMatters: Real dashboards routinely need to fetch several independent pieces of data in parallel (user profile, permissions, notifications, billing status) - using Promise.all when any failure should block the whole page, versus Promise.allSettled when you want to render whatever succeeded and show a partial error for what didn't, is a genuine architectural decision that affects perceived reliability and UX, not just a syntax choice.
realExample: A dashboard's landing page fetches user profile and auth permissions with Promise.all, since the whole page genuinely can't render meaningfully without both (fail fast, show a full error state), while its widget row (recent orders, usage graph, billing summary) uses Promise.allSettled so a single failing widget (e.g. a flaky billing microservice) shows an inline error card for just that widget while the other two widgets still render successfully with their own data.
commonMistake: Using Promise.all when independent widgets/sections should degrade gracefully instead of all failing together - one flaky endpoint then takes down the entire page's rendering, when allSettled would have let everything else still succeed and shown a localized error for just the failing piece.
interviewAnswer: A Promise is just a value that represents something that will resolve or reject eventually, and async/await is syntax that lets me write that code in a linear, synchronous-looking style with normal try/catch instead of chaining .then and .catch. For running multiple async operations together, the combinator I pick depends on the failure semantics I actually want - Promise.all if I genuinely need everything to succeed and want to fail fast otherwise, Promise.allSettled if I want to know the outcome of every one of them regardless of individual failures, which is usually the right choice for independent dashboard widgets so one flaky endpoint doesn't take down the whole page, and Promise.race or Promise.any for narrower cases like a timeout race or "whichever succeeds first."
followUps: What happens to the other promises in Promise.all if one of them rejects - do they keep running?
How would you implement a timeout for a fetch call using Promise.race?
What's the difference between an unhandled promise rejection and a caught one, in terms of runtime behavior?
miniExercise: Write a function fetchWithTimeout(url, ms) that races a fetch call against a timeout promise using Promise.race, rejecting with a clear timeout error if the fetch takes too long.
seniorDiscussion: Your dashboard's homepage currently uses Promise.all to fetch five independent widgets' data, and a single flaky endpoint occasionally blanks the entire page with an error screen instead of just that widget. Walk through migrating this to a more resilient pattern (allSettled, or per-widget fetching with independent loading/error state) and how you'd decide, per section, whether a failure should be page-blocking or gracefully degraded.

title: Error Handling Patterns
explanation: Robust error handling distinguishes between different failure types and handles each appropriately: expected/recoverable errors (a failed API validation, a declined payment) versus unexpected/programmer errors (a null reference bug), synchronous errors (try/catch) versus async errors (.catch, try/catch with await, or a global unhandledrejection listener as a safety net), and creating custom Error subclasses to carry structured context (status code, error code, field) rather than just a string message.
whyItMatters: Generic error handling ("just show an alert" or an empty catch block that swallows everything) is a major source of both bad UX and invisible production bugs - a payment failure that's silently swallowed instead of surfaced can mean a customer is charged inconsistently with what the UI shows, and an unhandled promise rejection in a critical flow can crash a whole feature with no diagnostic information reaching your error-tracking tool (Sentry, etc.).
realExample: A checkout flow's payment call throws a structured PaymentError with a code field (card_declined, insufficient_funds, network_error); the UI catches it and branches on err.code to show a specific, actionable message for each known case, while any error that isn't an instance of PaymentError (a genuine bug or unexpected failure) gets reported to an error-tracking service like Sentry and shown a generic "something went wrong, please try again" message instead of a technical stack trace.
commonMistake: Swallowing errors silently with an empty catch block (or catch (e) {}) "to stop the console from being noisy," which hides real production failures - including payment failures - from both users and your error-tracking tooling, making a serious bug look like it's simply not happening.
interviewAnswer: Good error handling starts with distinguishing expected, recoverable failures - a validation error, a declined card - from truly unexpected ones, like a null reference bug, because they deserve completely different treatment: expected errors get a specific, actionable message for the user, unexpected ones get reported to error tracking and a generic fallback message so I'm not leaking technical details. I like custom Error subclasses that carry structured data like a code or status field, so the UI can branch cleanly on err.code instead of doing fragile string matching on err.message. And the one thing I actively watch for in code review is a bare empty catch block - that silently swallows failures, which in something like a payment flow can mean a real problem goes completely unnoticed.
followUps: Why is catching errors by matching err.message a bad practice compared to a custom error code or class?
How would you set up a global handler for unhandled promise rejections as a safety net?
Should a UI ever show a raw error.message from the backend directly to the user? Why or why not?
miniExercise: Create a custom Error subclass ValidationError that carries a field name and message, then write a form-submit handler that catches it and displays the error next to the specific field, versus catching a generic Error and showing a top-level banner instead.
seniorDiscussion: Your payment integration (Stripe/Razorpay) can fail for many distinct reasons (card declined, insufficient funds, network timeout, fraud flag, webhook mismatch). How do you design the error-handling contract end-to-end - from the payment provider's error codes, through your backend's normalization, to a consistent set of UI states - so a new failure type discovered in production doesn't require a frontend code change to at least degrade gracefully?

title: Modules (ESM, CommonJS & Bundling Implications)
explanation: ES Modules (import/export) are statically analyzable at build time (imports/exports are fixed, not conditional), which is what enables tree-shaking - bundlers can determine exactly what's used and drop unused exports. CommonJS (require/module.exports), still common in older Node code and packages, is dynamic and resolved at runtime, which defeats most tree-shaking. Named exports vs default exports is also a real design choice: named exports are more tree-shake-friendly and give better auto-import/refactor tooling support, though defaults are common for a module's single primary export.
whyItMatters: Bundle size directly affects load performance, and tree-shaking only works reliably with ESM - a dependency shipped only as CommonJS, or code using dynamic/conditional require() calls, can silently bloat a production bundle because the bundler can't prove what's safe to remove. This is a real, recurring cause of "why is our bundle so big" investigations in mature frontend codebases.
realExample: A shared utils package exports dozens of small formatting/validation helpers as named ESM exports; a dashboard app imports only the three it actually uses (import { formatCurrency, formatDate, truncate } from "@acme/utils"), and because the package is published as ESM, the production bundler tree-shakes away the other 40+ unused exports entirely, keeping the shipped bundle lean despite the shared package being large.
commonMistake: Importing an entire library's default export or using a wildcard import (import * as utils from "big-lib") when only a couple of functions are needed, which can prevent effective tree-shaking depending on the library's module format and defeat the bundle-size benefit that named imports would have provided.
interviewAnswer: ES Modules are statically analyzable - the imports and exports are fixed at the top of the file, not computed at runtime - and that's exactly what lets a bundler tree-shake, meaning it can prove which exports are actually used and drop the rest from the final bundle. CommonJS's require/module.exports is dynamic and resolved at runtime, so a bundler generally can't safely tree-shake through it, which is a real, practical reason bundle sizes balloon when a dependency only ships CommonJS or a codebase mixes require() calls into otherwise-ESM code. In day-to-day work this mostly shows up as "why did adding this one import add 200kb to our bundle," and the answer is often exactly this - either the library isn't ESM, or it's being imported in a way that defeats tree-shaking.
followUps: Why can't a bundler safely tree-shake through a require() call the way it can through an ESM import?
What's the practical bundle-size difference between import * as _ from 'lodash' and importing individual lodash functions?
How would you investigate an unexpectedly large bundle size in a real project?
miniExercise: Using a bundle analyzer (or by reasoning through it manually), identify which of two import styles - import _ from 'lodash' followed by _.debounce(), versus import debounce from 'lodash/debounce' - results in a smaller production bundle, and explain why.
seniorDiscussion: Your team wants to add a large third-party analytics/charting library to the dashboard, and initial bundle analysis shows it adds 300kb even though only one chart type is actually used. What's your investigation and remediation plan - checking for ESM support and tree-shakeability, dynamic import() to code-split it, seeking a lighter alternative, or building a minimal wrapper around only the needed feature?

title: Iterators & Generators
explanation: An iterable is any object implementing Symbol.iterator (arrays, strings, Maps, Sets, and anything you define), which is what makes for...of and spread syntax work on it. A generator function (function*) is a convenient way to build an iterator - it can pause execution at each yield and resume later, maintaining internal state between calls, which is useful for lazy sequences (infinite or very large data you don't want to compute all at once) and for representing asynchronous workflows step-by-step before async/await existed for that purpose.
whyItMatters: Generators are less common in everyday app code but genuinely useful for specific real problems: lazily paginating through an API's results without loading everything into memory at once, implementing a custom iteration order over a complex data structure, or building the traversal logic behind a virtualized/windowed data table that only needs to compute the next visible chunk on demand rather than the entire dataset up front.
realExample: A large exportable report (e.g. "export all transactions") is generated using an async generator that yields one page of results at a time from the API, streaming each page directly into a CSV writer as it arrives, rather than fetching and holding tens of thousands of rows entirely in memory before starting to write the file - keeping memory usage flat regardless of the export's total size.
commonMistake: Reaching for a generator when a simple array method (map/filter) or a plain async function would do, adding unnecessary complexity and cognitive overhead for a case that doesn't actually need lazy evaluation or paused/resumable execution - generators are a specialized tool, not a general-purpose replacement for everyday iteration.
interviewAnswer: An iterable is anything implementing the Symbol.iterator protocol, which is what for...of and the spread operator actually rely on under the hood, and a generator function is the easiest way to build one - it can pause at a yield and resume later while keeping its own local state between pauses, unlike a normal function that starts fresh every call. In practice I reach for generators specifically when I need lazy evaluation - processing a huge or even infinite sequence one item at a time without loading it all into memory - like streaming pages of an API result set into a CSV export without holding the entire dataset in memory at once.
followUps: What's the difference between a regular iterator and an async iterator (for await...of)?
How would you build a custom iterable class (implementing Symbol.iterator manually) for a domain object like a linked list?
When would a generator be a worse choice than just returning a full array?
miniExercise: Write a generator function idGenerator() that lazily yields an infinite sequence of unique incrementing IDs, and demonstrate pulling just the first 5 values without ever computing more than needed.
seniorDiscussion: Your app needs to export a report that could contain millions of rows, currently implemented by fetching everything into a huge array and then writing a CSV, which occasionally crashes the browser tab on large exports. Would you move this to a generator-based streaming approach entirely client-side, move the heavy lifting server-side and stream the response to a file download, or use a Web Worker - and what's your reasoning for where the memory-heavy work should actually live?

title: Garbage Collection & Deep vs Shallow Copy
explanation: JS uses automatic garbage collection (primarily mark-and-sweep) - memory is reclaimed when an object becomes unreachable from any root reference, so memory leaks in JS are really "forgotten but still-reachable references" (a detached DOM node still referenced by a closure, an event listener never removed, a growing cache/array nobody clears) rather than manual memory mismanagement. Shallow copy ({ ...obj } or Object.assign) copies only the top level - nested objects/arrays still share references with the original - while deep copy (structuredClone, or a recursive/library approach) fully duplicates nested structures too.
whyItMatters: Memory leaks in long-lived single-page apps (a dashboard a user keeps open all day) are a real, senior-level production concern - event listeners attached to a removed component that are never cleaned up, or a growing in-memory cache of WebSocket messages that's never trimmed, can degrade performance over hours of use even though nothing looks wrong on a quick check. Shallow-vs-deep copy bugs are equally common: a "duplicate this row" feature that shallow-copies an object with a nested address field silently shares that nested object with the original, so editing the "duplicate" also mutates the original.
realExample: A "duplicate order" feature in an admin dashboard shallow-copies an order object to create a template for a new order, but the nested shippingAddress object is still the same reference as the original order's - editing the shipping address on the new draft order silently mutates the already-placed original order's address too, until the bug is caught and fixed by switching to structuredClone(order) for a real deep copy before any edits.
commonMistake: Assuming { ...obj } or Object.assign({}, obj) performs a full deep copy, when it only copies references for any nested object or array one level down - a very common source of "editing a copy also changed the original" bugs, especially with real-world domain objects that are rarely flat.
interviewAnswer: JS garbage collection is automatic, mostly mark-and-sweep - anything still reachable from a root (global scope, the call stack, active closures) survives, and anything unreachable eventually gets freed. So a "memory leak" in JS almost always means something is unintentionally still reachable - a common one is an event listener attached to a DOM node that never gets removed, keeping both the listener's closure and the node alive even after the node is visually gone, or an ever-growing cache that's never pruned. On copying, spread and Object.assign are shallow - they copy only the top-level properties, so any nested object or array is still shared by reference with the original, which causes real "editing the copy mutated the original" bugs unless you deliberately deep copy with something like structuredClone or a recursive utility.
followUps: How would you detect a memory leak in a long-running single-page app using devtools?
Why can event listeners specifically cause memory leaks, and how do you prevent it in a React component?
What's a scenario where structuredClone would fail or not be appropriate for deep copying?
miniExercise: Given a nested order object with a shippingAddress sub-object, write code that creates a true deep copy (not shallow) using structuredClone, then demonstrate that mutating the copy's nested address does not affect the original.
seniorDiscussion: Your team's dashboard has been reported by a few power users to slow down noticeably after being left open for several hours (a long-running SPA session, not a page reload). Walk through your investigation process using devtools' Memory panel (heap snapshots, detached DOM node detection, retained size) to find the leak, and describe two or three realistic root causes you'd check first in a React app with WebSocket connections and frequent re-renders.

title: Functional Programming Concepts & Design Patterns
explanation: Functional programming in JS emphasizes pure functions (same input always produces same output, no side effects), composition (building complex behavior from small functions combined together, e.g. pipe/compose), and avoiding shared mutable state - concepts that map directly onto how React encourages you to write components and hooks. Beyond FP, a handful of classic design patterns recur constantly in frontend code even without naming them explicitly: the Observer pattern (event emitters, React's own state subscriptions, RxJS), the Factory pattern (a createApiClient(config) function), and the Strategy pattern (swappable algorithms, like different validation or pricing strategies selected at runtime).
whyItMatters: Pure functions and composition make code dramatically easier to test (no mocking needed for a function with no side effects) and reason about (no hidden state to track), which is exactly why React pushes components and hooks toward being as close to pure functions of props/state as possible, and why "avoid side effects in the render body" is such a core React rule, not just a style preference. Recognizing design patterns by their real name also makes technical discussions and code reviews faster and more precise than reinventing ad hoc vocabulary each time.
realExample: A checkout flow's price calculation is built by composing small pure functions (applyDiscount, applyTax, applyShipping, roundToCents) with pipe, making each step independently unit-testable with plain input/output assertions and no mocking, while the actual discount logic itself uses a Strategy pattern - a lookup object mapping a promo code type to its calculation function - so adding a new discount type means adding one new pure function to the map, not editing a large branching if/else chain.
commonMistake: Writing "impure by default" functions that silently read or mutate outer state (a module-level variable, a shared mutable object passed by reference) instead of taking all their inputs as arguments and returning a new result - this makes unit testing require extensive setup/mocking and makes bugs dependent on call order, which is exactly the class of bug pure functions are designed to eliminate.
interviewAnswer: The core FP habits I lean on are pure functions - same inputs always give the same output, no hidden side effects - and composing small functions together instead of writing one large function that does everything, which is also just easier to unit test since there's no mocking required for something with no side effects. Beyond FP specifically, a few classic patterns show up in almost every frontend codebase whether or not people name them - the Observer pattern is basically what React's whole state-subscription model and any event-emitter or RxJS-based code is doing, and the Strategy pattern is what you're doing anytime you swap out an algorithm - like a pricing or validation rule - based on a runtime value using a lookup map instead of a long if/else chain.
followUps: Why does avoiding side effects in a function make it easier to unit test?
Give a concrete example of the Observer pattern already present in a React codebase without an explicit library.
When would introducing heavy FP abstraction (like a full pipe/compose utility library) be overkill for a small team?
miniExercise: Refactor a single large function that calculates a final order price with several nested if/else branches (discount, tax, shipping all inline) into a small set of pure functions composed together with a simple pipe utility, and write a unit test for just the discount function in isolation.
seniorDiscussion: Your team is debating whether to introduce a lightweight FP utility library (like Ramda or just hand-rolled pipe/compose helpers) versus keeping the codebase in a more "plain imperative JS/TS with occasional array methods" style. For a mid-size product team with mixed FP familiarity, how do you weigh the testability and composability benefits against the onboarding cost and potential over-abstraction risk?

title: Structural Typing
explanation: TypeScript uses structural typing (also called "duck typing" with static checks) - two types are compatible if their shapes match, regardless of name or declared relationship, unlike nominal typing (Java/C#) where types must explicitly share a name or inheritance chain. This means a function expecting { id: string; name: string } will happily accept any object with at least those properties, even one typed as a completely unrelated interface.
whyItMatters: Structural typing is what makes TypeScript flexible for real-world API integration - a response type from one endpoint can satisfy a parameter expecting a subset of its shape without any explicit casting or inheritance - but it also means "the types match" doesn't guarantee "this is semantically the right object," which trips up engineers coming from nominally-typed languages who expect stricter identity checks.
realExample: An API client function fetchEntity<T>(url: string): Promise<T> is called with both a User type and an Invoice type at different call sites; because TypeScript checks shape, not declared name, a response object that happens to satisfy an interface's required fields will type-check successfully even if it was never explicitly declared as that interface, which is powerful for flexibility but means a typo'd or mismatched API contract can slip through if the shapes coincidentally overlap.
commonMistake: Assuming that two differently-named interfaces being "type compatible" in TypeScript means they're semantically interchangeable in the domain - structural typing only checks shape, not intent, so a Product and a CartItem that happen to share the same three fields could be accidentally interchangeable in function signatures even though they represent completely different concepts.
interviewAnswer: TypeScript is structurally typed, meaning it checks the shape of a type, not its name or where it was declared - if an object has all the properties a function expects, it's considered compatible, even if it was typed as something else entirely. That's different from a nominally typed language like Java, where you'd need an explicit inheritance or interface implementation relationship. The upside is flexibility, especially with API responses that don't map one-to-one to your own domain types; the downside is that shape compatibility doesn't mean semantic correctness, so it's still possible to accidentally pass the wrong kind of object somewhere if the shapes happen to line up.
followUps: How does structural typing affect how you'd design two similar-but-distinct domain interfaces (like Product and CartItem) to avoid accidental interchangeability?
What's an example of a bug that structural typing would allow but nominal typing would catch?
How do branded/nominal types simulate nominal typing in TypeScript when you need it?
miniExercise: Define two interfaces, Employee { id: string; name: string } and Customer { id: string; name: string }, and demonstrate that a function expecting an Employee will accept an object typed as Customer, since TypeScript checks shape only - then discuss whether that's a problem for this specific pair of types.
seniorDiscussion: Your domain has two types, UserId and OrderId, both just strings under the hood, and structural typing means they're currently freely interchangeable - a bug lets an OrderId be passed where a UserId is expected with no compiler error. How would you use branded/nominal types (e.g. a unique symbol-based brand) to make these genuinely distinct at the type level, and is the added complexity worth it for your codebase?

title: Interfaces vs Type Aliases
explanation: interface and type can both describe object shapes and are largely interchangeable for that use case, but they differ in a few concrete ways: interfaces support declaration merging (multiple interface X {} declarations with the same name combine automatically) and are generally preferred for public API shapes/class contracts, while type aliases can represent unions, intersections, tuples, mapped types, and primitives directly, which interfaces cannot express on their own.
whyItMatters: Teams often adopt a convention (interface for object/component prop shapes, type for unions/utility compositions) purely for consistency, since the practical difference rarely matters for everyday component or API typing - but knowing exactly where they diverge (union types, declaration merging) is what separates "I copy whichever one I saw last" from an informed, defensible choice in code review.
simpleExample:
interface ButtonProps { label: string; onClick: () => void; } // object shape
