type Status = "idle" | "loading" | "success" | "error"; // union - interface can't do this
type ApiResult<T> = { data: T } | { error: string };      // union of object shapes
realExample: A component library defines all its component prop shapes with interface (e.g. interface TableProps<T>) for consistency and because consumers occasionally need to extend them via declaration merging for plugin-style customization, while the same codebase uses type for values like type SortDirection = "asc" | "desc" or type ApiResponse<T> = { status: "success"; data: T } | { status: "error"; message: string }, which are unions that interface syntax cannot express directly.
commonMistake: Trying to express a union type using interface (which isn't directly possible) and ending up with an awkward workaround, or conversely being unaware that only interface supports declaration merging, which matters when augmenting a third-party library's types (e.g. extending Express's Request type) where merging is required, not optional.
interviewAnswer: For plain object shapes, interface and type are basically interchangeable, and most teams just pick a convention - I tend to use interface for component props and public object contracts since it supports declaration merging, which matters for things like extending a third-party library's types, and I reach for type when I need a union, an intersection, or a mapped/conditional type, since interface genuinely can't express those on its own. It's a minor stylistic choice most of the time, but knowing the actual technical differences - not just 'type is newer' - is what lets you make a real decision instead of guessing.
followUps: What is declaration merging and when would you actually need it?
Can an interface extend a type alias, and vice versa?
Why might a component library specifically prefer interface for its public prop types?
miniExercise: Define a Status union type ("idle" | "loading" | "success" | "error") using type, then define a ButtonProps object shape using interface, and explain why you chose each construct for its specific use case.
seniorDiscussion: Your team is standardizing a lint rule to enforce either interface or type consistently for all object shapes across the codebase. What's your recommendation, and are there specific situations (declaration merging for augmenting third-party types, discriminated unions) where you'd carve out an explicit exception to the rule rather than enforcing it universally?

title: Unions & Intersections
explanation: A union type (A | B) means a value could be either type, and TypeScript requires you to narrow it (via a type guard) before accessing properties specific to just one branch. An intersection type (A & B) combines multiple types into one that must satisfy all of them simultaneously, useful for composing smaller shapes together (e.g. a base entity type intersected with a specific one) rather than duplicating shared fields across many interfaces.
whyItMatters: Unions map naturally onto real states a UI needs to represent - a request can be idle, loading, success, or error, and each state often carries different associated data (success has a data field, error has a message field); modeling this precisely with a discriminated union (rather than a single object with many optional fields) is what prevents impossible states like "loading and has error data" from being representable at all. Intersections are the practical way to compose shared fields (createdAt, id) across many domain types without copy-pasting them.
realExample: An API-response-handling hook types its state as a discriminated union RequestState<T> with a status field distinguishing idle/loading/success/error, each branch carrying only the fields relevant to that state (success has data, error has message) - this makes it a compile error to accidentally read state.data while status is "error", which a single flattened object with optional data?/error? fields would never catch, since both could technically coexist.
commonMistake: Modeling async/request state as one flat object with many optional fields (data?: T; error?: string; loading?: boolean) instead of a discriminated union, which allows impossible or contradictory states to type-check fine (loading: true and error: "x" and data: {...} all present simultaneously) even though the app logic never intends for that combination to occur.
interviewAnswer: A union means the value is one of several possible types, and I have to narrow it - usually by checking a common discriminant field - before TypeScript lets me safely access type-specific properties. An intersection combines multiple types into one that has to satisfy all of them, which I use a lot for composing shared fields, like a base entity with id and timestamps, into more specific domain types without repeating those fields everywhere. Where this really pays off is modeling async state - instead of one object with a bunch of optional data/error/loading fields that can technically all be true at once, a discriminated union with a status field makes impossible combinations, like 'loading and errored at the same time,' simply not type-check, which catches a whole category of bug before runtime.
followUps: What is a discriminated union and what specifically makes the discriminant field work for narrowing?
Why would modeling async request state as a single object with optional fields be considered worse than a discriminated union?
How does TypeScript narrow a union type inside a switch statement on the discriminant field?
miniExercise: Model the state of a payment form as a discriminated union with at least four states (idle, submitting, success with a transactionId, error with a message), and write a function that switches on the status field to render the right UI for each state with full type safety.
seniorDiscussion: Your team inherited a large codebase where async state is modeled as flat objects with data?, error?, and loading? all optional, leading to several real bugs from impossible-state combinations reaching production. How would you plan a migration to discriminated unions across dozens of existing components without a single giant risky PR - incremental type refactor, a shared generic RequestState<T> utility type, or a codemod?

title: Generics
explanation: Generics let you write reusable functions, types, and components that work across multiple types while preserving the specific type information for each call site, instead of falling back to any (losing all type safety) or writing a near-duplicate version per type. A generic type parameter (commonly T, but named meaningfully like TData or TItem in real code) is filled in either explicitly or inferred automatically from the arguments passed.
whyItMatters: Generics are what make a reusable useApi<TData>(url) hook, a generic Table<TRow> component, or a typed API client genuinely useful in a real codebase - without them, either every distinct data shape needs its own duplicated hook/component, or everything falls back to any and loses the type safety that's the entire point of using TypeScript.
realExample: A reusable DataTable<TRow> component accepts a columns: Column<TRow>[] prop and a data: TRow[] prop, so when it's used for an orders table (DataTable<Order>) versus a users table (DataTable<User>), TypeScript enforces that each column's accessor function correctly returns a type matching that specific row shape - catching a typo'd or mismatched column definition at compile time rather than as a runtime rendering bug.
commonMistake: Overusing a bare, unconstrained generic <T> where a specific union or interface would be clearer and safer, or reaching for any instead of a generic entirely "to make the error go away," which defeats the actual purpose of generics - preserving real type information across a reusable piece of code.
interviewAnswer: Generics let me write one reusable function or component that still keeps precise type information for each specific use, instead of either duplicating the same logic per type or giving up and using any. A good concrete example is a generic useApi<TData>(url) hook - the fetching logic is written once, but each call site gets back exactly the type it asked for, so useApi<User>() and useApi<Order[]>() are both fully type-safe without any duplicated code. I try to make sure the generic parameter is actually doing work - if a function doesn't need to preserve a caller-specific type, a generic there is just unnecessary complexity.
followUps: What's the difference between a generic constrained with extends and an unconstrained one?
How does TypeScript infer a generic type argument when you don't explicitly specify it?
When would using a generic be worse than just using a union type?
miniExercise: Write a generic function getProperty<T, K extends keyof T>(obj: T, key: K) that returns the correctly-typed value of a given property, and demonstrate that it correctly infers the return type based on which key is passed.
seniorDiscussion: Your team's generic DataTable<TRow> component has grown generic type parameters for columns, row actions, sorting, and filtering, each with their own constraints, and the type signature has become hard for new engineers to read. How do you balance genuinely useful type safety against generic-signature complexity that hurts developer experience - simplifying constraints, extracting named helper types, or accepting some any/unknown escape hatches at the boundaries?

title: Utility Types
explanation: TypeScript ships built-in utility types that transform existing types without redeclaring them: Partial<T> (all properties optional, useful for update/patch payloads), Required<T> (opposite), Pick<T, K> (select specific keys), Omit<T, K> (exclude specific keys), Record<K, V> (an object type with specified keys and value type), and Readonly<T> (all properties immutable at the type level). These let you derive precise, DRY types from a single source of truth instead of maintaining near-duplicate interfaces by hand.
whyItMatters: API payloads for creating vs updating vs displaying an entity are almost always slightly different shapes of the same underlying data (a create payload omits id/timestamps, an update payload makes most fields optional), and utility types let you derive all of these from one canonical entity type instead of manually maintaining three separate, drift-prone interfaces that all need updating together whenever a field changes.
simpleExample:
interface Invoice { id: string; amount: number; status: string; createdAt: string; }

type CreateInvoicePayload = Omit<Invoice, "id" | "createdAt">; // server assigns these
type UpdateInvoicePayload = Partial<Pick<Invoice, "amount" | "status">>; // patch a subset
type InvoiceSummary = Pick<Invoice, "id" | "amount" | "status">; // for a list view
realExample: A billing feature defines one canonical Invoice interface, then derives CreateInvoicePayload with Omit<Invoice, "id" | "createdAt"> (since the server assigns those), UpdateInvoicePayload with Partial<Pick<Invoice, "amount" | "status">> (a PATCH endpoint should only ever touch those two fields, and both are optional since a partial update might change just one), and an InvoiceSummary type with Pick<Invoice, "id" | "amount" | "status"> for a lightweight list view - all three stay automatically in sync if the base Invoice type changes.
commonMistake: Hand-maintaining several near-identical interfaces (Invoice, CreateInvoiceRequest, UpdateInvoiceRequest, InvoiceListItem) independently instead of deriving them from one source-of-truth type with Pick/Omit/Partial, which means adding or renaming a field requires remembering to update every duplicate manually, and they inevitably drift out of sync over time.
interviewAnswer: Utility types let me derive new types from one canonical type instead of hand-maintaining several near-duplicate interfaces. A common real example is an entity like Invoice - I'll derive a create-payload type with Omit to drop server-assigned fields like id, an update-payload type with Partial and Pick to allow patching just a subset of fields, and a summary type with Pick for a lighter list view. The benefit is that all of these stay in sync automatically if the base Invoice type changes, versus manually updating three or four separate interfaces every time a field is added or renamed, which is exactly how those types quietly drift apart in a real codebase.
followUps: What's the difference between Partial<T> and marking every field optional manually with '?'
How would you build your own utility type similar to Pick using mapped types?
When would Required<T> actually be useful in a real codebase?
miniExercise: Given a full User interface with id, name, email, role, and createdAt, derive a CreateUserPayload (no id/createdAt), an UpdateUserPayload (all fields optional except id), and a UserListItem (only id, name, role) - all using utility types, without redeclaring any fields manually.
seniorDiscussion: Your API's request/response types are currently hand-written and have drifted out of sync with the actual backend schema several times, causing runtime bugs that the type system didn't catch. Would you generate these utility-type-derived types from a shared schema (OpenAPI spec, tRPC, or a shared Zod schema used on both ends), and how does that change your team's source of truth for domain types going forward?

title: keyof, typeof & Indexed Access Types
explanation: keyof T produces a union of a type's property names as string literal types, useful for constraining a parameter to "must be a valid key of this object." typeof (in a type position) captures the type of an existing value/variable, useful for deriving a type from a runtime object (like a config or constants object) instead of declaring it twice. Indexed access types (T["propertyName"], or T[K] with a generic K extends keyof T) let you extract the type of a specific property, keeping derived types automatically in sync with the source.
whyItMatters: These three features together are what let you avoid "stringly-typed" bugs - a getProperty(obj, key) helper constrained with K extends keyof T catches a typo'd property name at compile time instead of returning undefined silently at runtime, and deriving a type from a real runtime object (typeof ROUTES) means your types can never drift out of sync with the actual constant they're describing.
realExample: A navigation helper derives its allowed route keys directly from a single ROUTES constants object using keyof typeof ROUTES, so adding, removing, or renaming a route in that one object automatically updates every place in the codebase that calls navigate(key) - the compiler immediately flags any call site referencing a route key that no longer exists, instead of a typo silently routing to undefined at runtime.
commonMistake: Manually declaring a union type or interface that's meant to mirror an existing object/constant (e.g. type RouteKey = "home" | "billing" | "settings" declared separately from the actual ROUTES object) instead of deriving it with keyof typeof, which means the two can silently drift out of sync whenever one is updated but not the other.
interviewAnswer: keyof takes an object type and gives me a union of its property names as literal types, which is great for constraining something like a "valid key of this object" parameter. typeof, when used in a type position rather than a value position, lets me capture the type of an existing runtime value, which is powerful combined with keyof - keyof typeof someConstObject gives me a union of that object's actual keys, derived automatically, so if the object changes, the type updates with it instead of drifting out of sync with a manually maintained duplicate. Indexed access types like T[K] then let me pull out the specific value type for a given key, which is exactly how a lot of strongly-typed config or routing helpers are built in real codebases.
followUps: Why is keyof typeof often preferable to manually writing a union type that mirrors an object's keys?
What's the difference between keyof on an interface versus keyof on a type derived with typeof?
How would you use an indexed access type to extract just the 'status' field's type from a larger Invoice interface?
miniExercise: Given a const FEATURE_FLAGS object with several boolean flag keys, derive a FeatureFlagKey type using keyof typeof, and write a function isEnabled(flag: FeatureFlagKey) that only accepts valid, existing flag names.
seniorDiscussion: Your app has a large, growing i18n translation keys object, and currently the type used to constrain translation key lookups is manually maintained and has drifted out of sync with the actual translations file several times, causing runtime "missing translation" bugs the compiler didn't catch. How would you use keyof typeof (or a codegen step) to make this impossible going forward, and what are the trade-offs if the translations object is extremely large (thousands of keys) for type-checking performance?

title: Type Narrowing, Guards & Discriminated Unions
explanation: Type narrowing is how TypeScript refines a broader type (a union, unknown, or a nullable type) down to a more specific one within a conditional block, based on runtime checks like typeof, instanceof, in, or an equality check against a discriminant field. A custom type guard is a function returning a special value is Type predicate, letting you encapsulate a more complex narrowing check (e.g. validating an API response shape) and reuse it while still getting proper narrowing at every call site.
whyItMatters: Correctly narrowing types (rather than using a type assertion/cast like as SomeType to silence the compiler) is what actually catches real bugs - especially for API responses (which arrive as unknown or a loosely-typed JSON blob) and for handling different branches of a discriminated union (like async request state or a payment result). A type assertion tells the compiler "trust me," which throws away exactly the safety net you were relying on TypeScript for in the first place.
realExample: A payment-processing response is typed as unknown right after being parsed from an external webhook payload; a custom type guard isPaymentSuccess(payload): payload is PaymentSuccess checks for the exact required fields and shape before the code proceeds to access payload.transactionId, ensuring a malformed or unexpected webhook payload (from a provider API change, or an attacker-crafted request) is caught and rejected instead of causing a runtime crash or, worse, silently processing incomplete data as if it were a successful payment.
commonMistake: Using an as Type assertion to silence a type error from the compiler instead of writing an actual runtime check/type guard - this compiles fine but provides zero real safety, since the assertion is just telling the compiler to trust a claim that's never actually verified at runtime, which is especially dangerous for untrusted external data like a webhook payload or API response.
interviewAnswer: Narrowing is how TypeScript lets me go from a broad type - a union, or unknown - down to something specific, based on an actual runtime check like typeof, instanceof, or checking a discriminant field, and within that narrowed block I get full type safety for the specific branch. For anything reused or non-trivial, I write a custom type guard - a function that returns a value is Type predicate - so the narrowing logic is centralized and testable, and every call site still gets properly narrowed types. The thing I actively avoid is reaching for an as Type assertion just to make a compiler error go away, because that's not actually checking anything at runtime - it's just telling the compiler to trust an unverified claim, which is especially risky for data coming from outside the app, like an API response or a payment webhook payload.
followUps: What's the difference between a type assertion (as Type) and a type guard (is Type)?
Why is validating an external API response with something like Zod often better than writing a hand-rolled type guard?
How does TypeScript narrow a discriminated union inside a switch statement automatically?
miniExercise: Write a custom type guard isInvoice(value: unknown): value is Invoice that checks all required fields exist with the correct primitive types, then use it to safely narrow a value: unknown before accessing its properties.
seniorDiscussion: Your app currently trusts API responses by casting them with as ApiResponseType at the network boundary, and a backend contract change recently caused a silent runtime bug that TypeScript didn't catch because the cast hid the mismatch. Would you introduce runtime schema validation (Zod, io-ts) at every API boundary, generate types directly from an OpenAPI/GraphQL schema to keep frontend and backend contracts in sync, or rely on stronger end-to-end contract testing - what's the right level of investment for your team's size and risk tolerance?

title: Enums & Alternatives, unknown, any & never
explanation: TypeScript's enum has real runtime footguns (numeric enums allow any number to be assigned even if it's not a valid member; enums generate actual JS objects at runtime, adding bundle size), which is why many teams prefer a union of string literals (type Status = "active" | "inactive") or an as const object instead, getting the same autocomplete/type-safety benefits with simpler runtime behavior. Separately, unknown is a type-safe version of any - it accepts anything but forces narrowing before use - any disables type checking entirely for a value, and never represents a value that can't occur (an exhaustive switch's default case, or a function that always throws).
whyItMatters: Choosing union literals over enum for status/mode-like values is a common, well-reasoned senior preference that shows real experience with TypeScript's rough edges, not just following a trend. Meanwhile, unknown versus any is a genuinely important distinction at any API/external-data boundary - typing a fetch response as any silently disables type checking for everything derived from it, while unknown forces you to prove the shape before using it, which is exactly the safety you want for untrusted external data.
realExample: A payment status field is typed as a string literal union type PaymentStatus = "pending" | "succeeded" | "failed" | "refunded" instead of an enum, avoiding the enum footgun where an invalid numeric value could otherwise be assigned without a compile error; a switch statement handling every PaymentStatus case ends its default branch with assertNever(status), so adding a new status value anywhere in the codebase produces an immediate compile error at every switch that isn't updated to handle it.
commonMistake: Typing an external API response as any "to make TypeScript stop complaining," which doesn't just skip checking that one value - it silently disables type checking for everything derived from it downstream too, since any is contagious through the type system, whereas unknown would have forced an explicit, safe narrowing step first.
interviewAnswer: I generally avoid TypeScript's enum in favor of a plain string literal union or an as const object, mainly because numeric enums have a real footgun - you can assign a number that isn't actually one of the defined members and the compiler won't catch it - and enums also generate real runtime code, adding to bundle size for something that's often just a compile-time concept. On the any-versus-unknown distinction, any completely disables type checking, and that unsafety is contagious through anything derived from that value, while unknown forces you to actually narrow the type before you can use it, which is exactly the safety I want when handling something like a raw API response. And never is genuinely useful for writing an exhaustiveness check - a helper that only accepts never lets a switch statement's default case guarantee, at compile time, that every union member is actually handled.
followUps: Why is a numeric enum considered unsafe compared to a string literal union?
How would you write an exhaustiveness check using the never type for a switch over a union?
What's a legitimate use case where enum might still be a reasonable choice?
miniExercise: Refactor a numeric enum OrderStatus { Pending, Shipped, Delivered } into a string literal union type, then write an assertNever-based exhaustiveness check for a switch statement handling all its values.
seniorDiscussion: Your codebase has years of accumulated enum usage across dozens of files, and the team wants to migrate to string literal unions for the reasons discussed, but a full rewrite is too risky to do at once. How would you sequence this migration - starting with new code only, a codemod for mechanical cases, or leaving stable/rarely-touched enums alone - and how do you avoid mixed inconsistency becoming its own long-term maintenance burden?

title: Function Overloads, Generic React Components & Advanced Types
explanation: Function overloads let a single function have multiple distinct type signatures for different argument combinations while sharing one implementation, useful when a function's return type genuinely depends on which arguments were passed in a way generics alone can't cleanly express. Generic React components (function Table<TRow>(props: TableProps<TRow>)) extend this to component APIs, preserving row/item type safety through props like columns and data. Mapped types ({ [K in keyof T]: ... }) and conditional types (T extends U ? X : Y) let you programmatically derive new types from existing ones - the mechanism behind many utility types themselves.
whyItMatters: These are genuinely advanced, senior-level TypeScript tools - most day-to-day code doesn't need them, but a shared component library, a form-typing system, or an API-client generator often does, and knowing when reaching for them is worth the added complexity (versus when a simpler union or a couple of overloaded utility functions would be clearer) is itself a sign of TypeScript maturity, not just familiarity with syntax.
realExample: A shared form library's useField<TValue> hook uses function overloads so calling it with just a field name infers TValue as string by default, while calling it with an explicit generic argument (useField<number>("amount")) or a schema-derived type gives full type safety for non-string fields - letting simple text-input cases stay ergonomic while still supporting fully-typed numeric, date, or enum fields without a completely separate API.
commonMistake: Reaching for a complex mapped/conditional type or a generic-heavy component API when a simpler, more explicit union type or a couple of overloaded functions would communicate the same constraint far more readably - advanced type-level programming should solve a real, recurring problem in a shared library, not be used as a showcase of TypeScript cleverness that the rest of the team then struggles to read or extend.
interviewAnswer: Function overloads let one function present multiple distinct call signatures - different argument shapes producing genuinely different return types - while still having one shared implementation underneath, which comes up in things like a shared form or query hook where the caller's exact usage pattern determines the most precise return type. Generic components extend the same idea to React - a Table<TRow> component keeps full type safety for whatever row type the caller passes in, rather than falling back to any for a fully reusable component. Mapped and conditional types are the actual mechanism a lot of built-in utility types are implemented with, and I'd reach for them directly in a shared library or design system when I need to derive a genuinely new type shape programmatically - but for regular day-to-day application code, I'd rather use a simpler, explicit type than write my own conditional type just because it's possible.
followUps: When would you reach for function overloads instead of a single function accepting a union parameter?
How would you write a mapped type that makes every property of an interface nullable?
What's the risk of over-engineering a shared component's generic type signature, and how would you recognize you've gone too far?
miniExercise: Write a generic function getFirst that has two overloads: one that returns T | undefined for a plain array, and one that returns a more specific type when passed a non-empty tuple type, demonstrating how overloads let the same function name express different guarantees based on its input.
seniorDiscussion: Your design system's generic Table<TRow> component's type signature has grown increasingly complex - conditional types for optional row-selection support, mapped types for column configuration, and several overloads for different data-fetching modes - to the point where new engineers regularly get confused by cryptic generic type errors. How do you rebalance flexibility against usability here - simplifying the public type surface even if it means slightly less precise inference, adding better error messages via typed helper utilities, or splitting it into multiple simpler components instead of one maximally flexible one?

title: API Response & Form Typing + tsconfig Fundamentals
explanation: Typing API responses well means treating the network boundary as untrusted - defining a precise response type, and ideally validating it at runtime with a schema library (Zod) rather than just casting - and typing forms well usually means deriving the form's TypeScript type directly from the same validation schema (z.infer<typeof schema>) so the form's types and its validation rules can never drift apart. Separately, tsconfig.json controls how strict the compiler actually is - strict: true (which itself enables noImplicitAny, strictNullChecks, and others) is the single most impactful setting, since disabling it silently reintroduces most of the bugs TypeScript exists to prevent.
whyItMatters: A huge number of real production bugs come from a backend contract silently changing (a field renamed, a type changed from string to number) that a plain TypeScript interface - checked only at compile time, against fake/assumed data - can't catch, because TypeScript provides zero runtime guarantees. Combining Zod (runtime validation) with type inference from that same schema is how senior engineers close this exact gap, and it's also what powers most modern typed-form libraries (React Hook Form + zodResolver) end to end.
realExample: A checkout form defines a single Zod schema for the payment details (amount, currency, cardholder name), uses z.infer to derive the exact TypeScript type React Hook Form's useForm<PaymentFormData>() needs, and reuses the same schema both for the form's client-side validation (via zodResolver) and for validating the API response/request payload server-side - so the form's types, its validation rules, and the API contract are all derived from one single source of truth instead of three independently-maintained versions that can drift.
commonMistake: Turning off strict mode (or specific strict flags like strictNullChecks) in tsconfig.json to make a legacy codebase's type errors "go away" quickly, which silently reintroduces null/undefined-related runtime crashes and implicit any leaks throughout the codebase - exactly the class of bug the compiler's strict mode exists to catch in the first place.
interviewAnswer: For API responses and forms, I try to have one real source of truth rather than separate hand-maintained types for each - typically a Zod schema, since I can derive the TypeScript type from it with z.infer and also use the exact same schema to actually validate data at runtime, whether that's a form submission or a raw API response. That closes a real gap, because plain TypeScript interfaces give you zero runtime protection - they only check code you write against assumed shapes, not the actual data arriving over the network, which is exactly where backend contract changes silently break things. On tsconfig, strict: true is the setting I'd never disable just to silence errors quickly, because it bundles together things like strictNullChecks and noImplicitAny that catch a huge share of real runtime bugs at compile time - turning it off to make errors disappear just means those same bugs resurface at runtime instead.
followUps: Why does a TypeScript interface alone provide zero runtime safety for an API response?
What specific checks does strict: true actually enable in tsconfig, and which one do you consider most valuable?
How would you keep a Zod schema and a corresponding database/backend type in sync over time?
miniExercise: Define a Zod schema for a simple signup form (email, password, confirmPassword with a refinement that they match), derive its TypeScript type with z.infer, and wire it into a React Hook Form using zodResolver so validation errors and form types both come from the same schema.
seniorDiscussion: Your team inherited a legacy codebase with strict: false in tsconfig and thousands of resulting implicit any usages and unchecked null accesses. How would you plan a path to strict: true - enabling individual strict flags incrementally (strictNullChecks first, then noImplicitAny), using // @ts-expect-error suppressions temporarily with a tracked cleanup backlog, or file-by-file migration - given that a big-bang switch would likely produce thousands of errors at once?

title: Component Model, JSX, Props & State
explanation: A React component is a function that takes props (read-only, passed from a parent) and returns JSX describing what the UI should look like given that data. State (via useState or similar) is data a component owns and can change over time, and updating state triggers a re-render. The core mental model is unidirectional data flow: data flows down through props, and events flow up through callbacks passed as props, rather than children reaching up to mutate a parent directly.
whyItMatters: Almost every React bug and design question traces back to this model: "where should this piece of state live" (in the component that needs it, or lifted to a shared ancestor), "why isn't my UI updating" (state wasn't actually changed, or props aren't flowing where expected), and "why does this child need a callback prop instead of directly changing something" are all direct consequences of props-down/events-up being the intended architecture, not an arbitrary restriction.
realExample: An orders table renders each row as an OrderRow component receiving order data as props and an onStatusChange callback prop; when a row's "Mark Shipped" button is clicked, the row doesn't mutate anything itself - it calls onStatusChange(order.id, "shipped"), which the parent table (or a data-fetching layer above it) uses to actually update the underlying order data and trigger a re-render with the new status, keeping data flow predictable and traceable.
commonMistake: Trying to have a child component directly mutate data owned by a parent (or reach into a parent's state) instead of calling a callback prop the parent provided - this breaks the unidirectional data flow model that makes React apps predictable to reason about, and usually signals that state needs to be lifted to a common ancestor instead.
interviewAnswer: A React component is really just a function of its props that returns JSX describing the UI for a given input, and state is data the component itself owns that can change over time and triggers a re-render when it does. The model I always come back to is props flow down, events flow up - a child never directly reaches into or mutates its parent's data, it calls a callback prop the parent handed it, and the parent decides what to actually do with that event, including updating its own state. Most 'why isn't this updating' or 'where should this state live' questions in React resolve once you're clear on that direction of data flow.
followUps: When should a piece of state be lifted up to a parent versus kept local to a component?
What's the practical difference between props and state in terms of who can change them?
Why does calling a setState function trigger a re-render, but mutating a plain variable doesn't?
miniExercise: Build a small ExpandableRow component that receives a title and content as props, manages its own expanded/collapsed boolean as local state, and calls an onToggle(isExpanded) callback prop whenever it changes - demonstrating both local state and props-based communication with a parent.
seniorDiscussion: For a complex table with row selection, sorting, and inline editing, where does each piece of state genuinely belong - inside each row component, lifted to the table, lifted further to a page-level state manager, or pushed into the URL/query params - and what's your framework for making that call consistently across a team?

title: Controlled vs Uncontrolled Components
explanation: A controlled component has its value fully driven by React state (value + onChange), making React the single source of truth, while an uncontrolled component keeps its own internal DOM state and you read it on demand via a ref (or a library like React Hook Form, which uses uncontrolled inputs under the hood by default for performance). Controlled gives you instant access to the current value for validation/formatting on every keystroke; uncontrolled avoids a re-render per keystroke, which matters for very large or performance-sensitive forms.
whyItMatters: Large real-world forms (checkout, multi-field onboarding, a settings page with dozens of fields) can suffer real performance problems if every field is a fully controlled input causing a re-render on every keystroke across the whole form tree - this is exactly why React Hook Form defaults to uncontrolled inputs with refs, only wiring up controlled behavior where actually needed (e.g. a custom Select or a value that needs live formatting like a currency field).
realExample: A 40-field employee onboarding form uses React Hook Form's uncontrolled-by-default inputs (register()) so typing in any single field doesn't re-render the other 39, while a currency amount field specifically needs to be controlled (via Controller) because it must reformat the displayed value live as the user types (adding thousand separators), which requires React to own and reformat the value on every change.
commonMistake: Making every single input in a large form fully controlled by default (a useState per field, or a naive single big controlled state object triggering a full form re-render on every keystroke) without a real reason, when an uncontrolled approach (or a form library defaulting to uncontrolled) would avoid unnecessary re-renders for fields that don't need live validation or formatting.
interviewAnswer: Controlled means React state is the source of truth for an input's value - you pass value and onChange, and the input only shows what state says it should. Uncontrolled means the DOM itself holds the current value, and you reach in with a ref only when you actually need to read it, which avoids a re-render on every keystroke. For a small form I'd usually just use controlled inputs since it's simpler to reason about, but for a large form with many fields, I'd lean uncontrolled by default - which is exactly why React Hook Form uses uncontrolled inputs under the hood - and only make a specific field controlled when it genuinely needs live behavior, like reformatting a currency value as you type.
followUps: Why does React Hook Form default to uncontrolled inputs, and what's the performance reasoning?
How would you make a specific field within an otherwise-uncontrolled form controlled (e.g. for live formatting)?
What are the trade-offs of controlled inputs for accessibility or testing purposes?
miniExercise: Build the same text input two ways - fully controlled with useState, and uncontrolled using a ref and defaultValue - and use the React DevTools Profiler to compare how many times the component (and its siblings) re-render while typing in each version.
seniorDiscussion: Your team's design system needs a single Input component that works well both in simple controlled use cases (a filter bar) and inside large uncontrolled forms managed by React Hook Form. How do you design its API (value/onChange vs defaultValue/ref forwarding, or supporting both) so it's genuinely reusable across both patterns without the component needing to know which mode it's in?

title: Rendering Lifecycle, Reconciliation, Virtual DOM & Keys
explanation: React re-renders a component when its state or props change, producing a new virtual DOM tree (a lightweight JS representation), then diffs it against the previous tree (reconciliation) to compute the minimal set of real DOM mutations needed, rather than re-rendering the entire page to the actual DOM every time. For lists, the key prop tells React which items are the "same" across renders so it can correctly match, reorder, add, or remove DOM nodes instead of guessing by position - a missing or unstable key (like array index for a reorderable list) causes real, sometimes hard-to-spot bugs.
whyItMatters: Getting keys wrong is one of the most common real React bugs: using array index as a key for a list that can be reordered, filtered, or have items inserted/removed causes React to incorrectly reuse DOM nodes (and their internal component state) for the wrong logical item - a classic symptom is a text input inside a reorderable list showing the wrong value after a reorder, because React matched it to the wrong item by position, not identity.
realExample: A sortable orders table lets users click a column header to re-sort the rows; using order.id as the key ensures React correctly matches each OrderRow to its actual underlying order across the re-sort (preserving any row-local state like an "expanded details" toggle correctly attached to the right row), whereas using the array index as key would have caused expanded/collapsed state to appear to "jump" to the wrong rows after sorting, since index-based identity doesn't track the actual data.
commonMistake: Using the array index as a list's key prop for any list that can be reordered, filtered, or have items added/removed in the middle - this is a very common but subtly broken pattern that appears to work fine until the list actually changes order or membership, at which point component state and DOM nodes get mismatched to the wrong logical items.
interviewAnswer: React re-renders a component whenever its state or props change, but instead of touching the real DOM directly on every render, it builds a lightweight virtual representation and diffs it against the previous one to figure out the smallest actual set of DOM changes needed - that diffing process is reconciliation. For lists specifically, React needs a stable key to know which item is which across renders, since without a real identity it can only guess by position, and that guess breaks the moment a list gets reordered, filtered, or has an item inserted in the middle - the classic bug is using the array index as the key, which appears to work until the list actually changes, at which point component state and DOM nodes get silently matched to the wrong item.
followUps: Why specifically does using array index as a key break for a reorderable or filterable list, but work fine for a static, append-only list?
What's the difference between the virtual DOM and reconciliation - are they the same thing?
How does React decide whether to reuse or recreate a DOM node when a component's type changes between renders?
miniExercise: Build a reorderable list (e.g. drag handles or up/down buttons) where each item contains a local text input, first using array index as the key, then switching to a stable id-based key - demonstrate the bug the index-based version has after reordering, and confirm the id-based version fixes it.
seniorDiscussion: Your team has a large, deeply nested component tree (a dashboard with many widgets, each with their own state) and re-renders are causing noticeable frame drops during rapid data updates. Walk through how you'd use React DevTools Profiler to distinguish between "necessary re-renders that are just expensive" versus "unnecessary re-renders that shouldn't be happening at all," and what different fixes each diagnosis would call for.

title: Synthetic Events, Lifting State & Composition
explanation: React wraps native DOM events in a cross-browser-consistent SyntheticEvent object, attached (in modern React) at the root and dispatched through React's own event system rather than one native listener per element - this is what makes event handling behave consistently across browsers and interacts with React's batching of state updates. "Lifting state up" means moving state from a child to the closest common ancestor of every component that needs to read or change it, when two siblings need to share or coordinate state. Composition (passing components as children/props, rather than configuring one giant component with many boolean props) is React's preferred alternative to deep prop-drilling or over-configurable components.
whyItMatters: Real dashboards constantly need sibling components to coordinate - a filter panel and a data table that must stay in sync, a set of linked charts that all respond to the same date-range selector - and lifting state to their common parent (rather than each owning its own disconnected copy) is the correct, idiomatic React solution to this coordination problem, well before reaching for a global state library. Composition-based APIs (a Modal component that accepts arbitrary children, versus a Modal with 15 boolean/variant props) also scale much better as product requirements grow.
realExample: A dashboard's date-range picker, revenue chart, and orders table all need to reflect the same selected date range; rather than each having its own independent date state (which would desync immediately), the dateRange state is lifted to the shared Dashboard parent and passed down as props to all three, so changing the range in one place instantly and correctly updates the other two - a direct, idiomatic application of lifting state up instead of introducing a global store just to coordinate three sibling components.
commonMistake: Reaching immediately for a global state library (Redux/Zustand/Context) to coordinate two or three sibling components that could simply share state via their nearest common parent - premature global state adds indirection and complexity for a coordination problem that lifting state up already solves cleanly and locally.
interviewAnswer: React wraps native browser events in its own SyntheticEvent so event handling behaves consistently across browsers, and in modern React these are dispatched through a root-level listener rather than one native listener per element, which also ties into how React batches state updates from event handlers. On architecture, when two sibling components need to share or coordinate state - like a date-range picker and the chart and table that both depend on it - the right first move is usually just lifting that state up to their nearest common parent, not reaching for a global store, since the coordination problem is genuinely local. And when a component's API is getting overloaded with configuration props to handle every visual variant, that's usually a sign to switch to composition - passing children or slot-like props - instead of one increasingly complex, over-configured component.
followUps: When does lifting state up stop being sufficient, and you should reach for Context or a state library instead?
What's an example of a component that should be refactored from a 'many boolean props' API to a composition-based API?
How does event delegation/batching in React's synthetic event system affect when a state update actually triggers a re-render?
miniExercise: Refactor two sibling components that each maintain their own separate, out-of-sync `selectedTab` state into a single shared state lifted to their common parent, passed down as props to both.
seniorDiscussion: Your dashboard's filter state (date range, category, search term) is shared across five different widgets and is starting to need to be lifted quite high up the tree, causing a lot of prop drilling through intermediate components that don't otherwise care about it. At what point do you introduce Context (or a lightweight state library) instead of continuing to lift state, and how do you decide the right boundary so you don't over-centralize state that's actually fine staying local?

title: Custom Hooks
explanation: A custom hook is just a regular function, prefixed with use by convention, that itself calls other hooks (useState, useEffect, etc.) internally - it's the primary mechanism for extracting and reusing stateful logic across components without duplicating code or resorting to older patterns like render props or higher-order components. The Rules of Hooks (only call at the top level, only from React functions or other hooks) apply to custom hooks exactly the same way, since they're built from the same primitives under the hood.
whyItMatters: Real codebases accumulate custom hooks for exactly the recurring problems that show up across features - useDebounce, usePagination, useWebSocket, useLocalStorage, usePermission(role) - extracting these once and reusing them everywhere is both a huge DRY win and, done well, becomes a genuine internal API that encodes your team's best practices (like always cancelling a fetch on unmount) in one place instead of every engineer reimplementing it slightly differently.
realExample: A search-as-you-type feature across three different dashboard pages (orders, customers, products) all use the same useDebouncedValue hook to delay firing an API call until the user pauses typing, instead of each page independently reimplementing its own setTimeout/cleanup logic slightly differently - centralizing it in one hook also means a later fix (like properly cancelling the in-flight request too) benefits every usage at once.
commonMistake: Extracting a custom hook purely to "follow the pattern" for logic that's only used in one place and isn't likely to be reused, adding a layer of indirection without a real benefit - custom hooks are most valuable for genuinely shared, non-trivial stateful logic, not as a mandatory wrapper for every single useState/useEffect pair.
interviewAnswer: A custom hook is really just a normal function that happens to call other hooks internally, and the use prefix is a convention that lets both linters and other engineers know it follows the Rules of Hooks - same restrictions as any built-in hook, called only at the top level of a component or another hook. The value is extracting real, reusable stateful logic - something like debouncing a value, managing a WebSocket connection with reconnect logic, or checking a permission - once, in one well-tested place, instead of every feature reimplementing a slightly different, slightly buggier version of the same thing. I try not to over-apply this though - if a piece of state/effect logic is only ever used in one component and isn't likely to be reused, wrapping it in a custom hook just adds a layer of indirection for no real benefit.
followUps: What are the Rules of Hooks, and why do they exist (what would break if you called a hook conditionally)?
How would you test a custom hook in isolation, without mounting a full component?
When is extracting a custom hook not worth it?
miniExercise: Write a custom hook usePrevious(value) that returns the previous render's value of whatever is passed in (using a ref internally), and use it to detect when a specific prop transitions from one value to another.
seniorDiscussion: Your team has accumulated dozens of custom hooks over time, several of which do very similar things slightly differently (three different debounce hooks, two different "fetch with loading/error state" hooks). How do you audit and consolidate a hook library like this without breaking existing usages across a large codebase, and what process would you put in place to prevent this duplication from recurring?

title: useState, useEffect & useRef
explanation: useState holds a piece of state that persists across renders and triggers a re-render when updated (and updates can be batched, or can use a function form to safely update based on the previous value). useEffect runs a side effect after render, re-running whenever any value in its dependency array changes, and its optional cleanup function runs before the next effect execution and on unmount - critical for cancelling subscriptions, timers, or in-flight requests. useRef holds a mutable value that persists across renders without triggering a re-render when changed, commonly used for direct DOM access or for storing a value you need to read/write without caring about re-rendering.
whyItMatters: These three hooks cover the overwhelming majority of real component logic, and their subtleties are exactly what senior engineers get right and juniors often get wrong: forgetting an effect's cleanup function causes memory leaks and duplicate subscriptions (especially costly for a live WebSocket connection or a real-time chart), and using useRef versus useState for the wrong purpose either causes unnecessary re-renders or a UI that silently fails to update when it should.
realExample: A live order-updates WebSocket connection is opened inside a useEffect keyed on the current organization ID, with a cleanup function that explicitly closes the socket - this prevents the extremely common real-time-dashboard bug where switching organizations (or the component re-rendering) leaves the old socket connection open in the background, silently duplicating incoming messages or leaking memory over a long session.
commonMistake: Forgetting the cleanup function in a useEffect that sets up a subscription, timer, or WebSocket connection - each re-render (or unmount/remount, like navigating away and back) creates a new one without tearing down the old one, leading to duplicate event handling, memory leaks, and increasingly strange bugs the longer a session runs.
interviewAnswer: useState gives a component a piece of state that persists across renders and triggers a re-render whenever it's updated - and I use the function form, setX(prev => ...), whenever the new value depends on the previous one, to avoid stale-value bugs. useEffect runs after render and re-runs whenever something in its dependency array changes, and I treat its cleanup function as non-optional for anything that sets up an ongoing subscription, timer, or connection - a WebSocket, an event listener, an interval - because without cleanup, every re-render or remount can silently stack up duplicate versions of that thing running in the background. useRef is for anything I need to persist across renders without triggering a re-render when it changes - a DOM node reference, or a mutable value like 'the latest callback' that effects need to read without becoming a dependency.
followUps: Why does forgetting a useEffect cleanup function specifically cause problems for WebSocket connections or event listeners, but not for a one-time fetch?
When would you choose useRef over useState for storing a value?
What's the difference between the dependency array being empty, omitted, or containing specific values?
miniExercise: Build a component that opens a WebSocket connection (or a mock interval simulating one) inside a useEffect keyed on a changing prop, with proper cleanup, and demonstrate (by logging) that switching the prop value correctly closes the old connection before opening a new one.
seniorDiscussion: Your dashboard has a live-updating chart subscribing to a WebSocket, and under certain navigation patterns (rapidly switching between two tabs) you're seeing duplicate data points appear, suggesting multiple socket connections are alive simultaneously. Walk through your debugging process for confirming this diagnosis (using devtools' Network/WS tab and React DevTools) and the fix, and discuss whether the real issue is likely a missing cleanup function, an unstable dependency array causing the effect to re-run more than intended, or something else entirely.

title: useMemo, useCallback & React.memo
explanation: useMemo memoizes an expensive computed value across renders (only recomputing when its dependencies change), useCallback memoizes a function reference itself (useful specifically to keep a stable reference for a callback passed to a memoized child or as another hook's dependency), and React.memo wraps a component so it skips re-rendering when its props are shallow-equal to the previous render. None of these are free - they add memory and comparison overhead - so the senior-level skill is knowing when they actually prevent a real, measured performance problem versus when they're premature optimization that adds complexity for no measurable benefit.
whyItMatters: Overusing useMemo/useCallback/React.memo "just in case" is extremely common and often actively counterproductive - wrapping everything adds real overhead (the dependency comparison itself costs something) and cognitive load, without fixing anything, because a component was never actually re-rendering unnecessarily or the render itself was cheap. These tools earn their keep specifically around genuinely expensive computations, or components with expensive renders, in large lists or deeply nested trees where profiling has actually shown a problem.
realExample: A dashboard renders a table of 5,000 orders with an expensive client-side sort/filter recomputed on every render; wrapping that computation in useMemo (keyed on the actual orders/filter/sort-field dependencies) avoids re-sorting on every unrelated parent re-render (like a sidebar toggle), while each OrderRow is wrapped in React.memo and receives a useCallback-stabilized onClick handler, so scrolling or toggling an unrelated UI element doesn't re-render all 5,000 rows - verified by profiling before and after, not applied blindly.
commonMistake: Wrapping every function in useCallback and every component in React.memo by default, without profiling first to confirm there's an actual, measurable re-render problem - since the memoization comparison itself has a cost, and if the underlying component's render was already cheap, this "optimization" often makes the code both slower (marginally) and harder to read for zero real benefit.
interviewAnswer: useMemo caches an expensive computed value so it isn't redone on every render unless its inputs change, useCallback does the same thing but for a function's identity, which matters specifically when that function is a dependency somewhere else or is being passed to a component wrapped in React.memo, and React.memo itself skips a component's re-render entirely if its props are shallow-equal to last time. The important discipline here is that none of these are free - they all add some overhead - so I only reach for them after actually profiling and confirming a real, expensive re-render is happening, typically on a large list or a genuinely heavy computation, rather than sprinkling them everywhere by default as a habit.
followUps: Why does wrapping a function in useCallback not help at all unless it's also passed to a memoized child or used as another hook's dependency?
What's a concrete example of useMemo actually making performance worse?
How would you use the React DevTools Profiler to justify adding React.memo to a specific component?

title: useReducer & Context API
explanation: useReducer manages complex state transitions through a single reducer function (state, action) => newState, which is often clearer than several interrelated useState calls when state updates depend on each other or follow well-defined transitions (like a multi-step form or an async request's idle/loading/success/error states). Context provides a way to pass data through the component tree without manually threading props through every intermediate level (prop drilling), but it is not a general-purpose state management replacement - every context value change re-renders every consumer, which can become a real performance problem if a context holds fast-changing or unrelated pieces of state together.
whyItMatters: useReducer + Context is a common, framework-native pattern for medium-complexity shared state (like a shopping cart, a multi-step form wizard, or a theme/permission context) without pulling in an external state library - but conflating "Context solves prop drilling" with "Context is a performant global state manager" is a very common mistake that causes real, hard-to-diagnose re-render performance problems once an app grows past a certain size.
realExample: An RBAC-aware app provides the current user's role and permission set via a PermissionContext at the root, so any deeply nested component (a button three levels down in a settings page) can call useContext(PermissionContext) directly to check access instead of that data being manually threaded as props through every intermediate layout/wrapper component that doesn't otherwise care about permissions.
commonMistake: Putting frequently-changing, high-frequency state (like live cursor position, a per-keystroke form value, or real-time WebSocket data) into a single large Context that many unrelated components consume - since any change to the context value re-renders every consumer regardless of whether it actually cares about that specific piece of data, this can cause serious, hard-to-trace performance problems as the app scales.
interviewAnswer: useReducer is useful once state transitions get complex enough that several useState calls would need to be updated together in a coordinated way - a reducer centralizes exactly what each action does to the state in one place, which reads a lot like a small state machine and is genuinely clearer for something like a multi-step form or async request lifecycle. Context solves a real but narrower problem - avoiding prop drilling through many layers that don't otherwise care about a piece of data, like a current user or theme - but it's not a performant general state manager, since updating a context value re-renders every single consumer regardless of whether that specific consumer needed that specific change, which is exactly why I'd avoid putting fast-changing or unrelated pieces of state into one big shared context.
followUps: Why does every consumer of a Context re-render on any change to that context's value, and how would you mitigate that for a large app?
When would useReducer be a better choice than several separate useState calls?
How would you split one large Context into several smaller ones to reduce unnecessary re-renders?
miniExercise: Model a multi-step checkout form's state (current step, shipping info, payment info, and a status field) using useReducer with distinct action types for each transition, and write the reducer so an invalid action (unrecognized type) returns the state unchanged with a warning logged.
seniorDiscussion: Your app currently has one large AppContext holding user info, theme, notifications, and live WebSocket data all together, and profiling shows components re-rendering far more often than they should because of unrelated updates to that single context. How would you restructure this - splitting into multiple smaller, purpose-specific contexts, moving fast-changing data out of Context entirely (into a dedicated state library or a ref-based subscription pattern), or something else - and how do you prioritize which piece to fix first given limited time?

title: Stale Closures, Effect Cleanup & Race Conditions
explanation: A stale closure happens when a function (an effect, an event handler, a callback passed to a child) captures an old value of a prop or state variable from a previous render, because the closure was created before that value updated and the dependency array (or lack thereof) didn't cause it to be recreated with the fresh value. A race condition in data fetching happens when multiple async requests are in flight and resolve out of order - an earlier, slower request's response arrives after a later, faster request's, silently overwriting the correct, more recent data with stale results, unless you explicitly guard against it (an AbortController, or checking a request is still the "current" one before applying its result).
whyItMatters: These are two of the most common, hardest-to-reproduce bugs in real React apps - a stale closure bug might only manifest intermittently depending on exact render timing, and a fetch race condition might only be visible on a slow network or when a user types/navigates quickly (e.g. changing filters rapidly on a data table) - both classes of bug are frequently missed in code review and only surface in production or under specific network conditions during QA.
realExample: A data table's filter dropdown triggers a new fetch on every change; without a cancellation guard, quickly switching from "Pending" to "Completed" to "Refunded" could show Refunded-filtered results briefly, then have them silently overwritten by the slower "Pending" request's response arriving late - the fix uses a cancelled flag (or AbortController) inside the effect's cleanup so only the response matching the current, latest filterId is ever applied to state.
commonMistake: Fetching data inside a useEffect on every dependency change without any cancellation or "is this still the current request" guard, assuming responses will always arrive in the same order requests were sent - network timing makes zero such guarantee, and this is a very common, real production bug in filterable/searchable data tables.
interviewAnswer: A stale closure happens when a callback or effect was created capturing an older value of some state or prop, and something later changes that value, but the already-created closure still only sees the value it captured at creation time - this is exactly what the exhaustive-deps lint rule is trying to protect against, by making sure your dependency array actually reflects everything the effect closes over. A race condition in fetching is a separate but related class of bug - if a user changes a filter quickly, an earlier, slower request can resolve after a newer, faster one, silently overwriting the correct data with stale results unless you explicitly guard against it, typically with a cancelled flag in the effect's cleanup function or an AbortController tied to the request.
followUps: Why does the exhaustive-deps ESLint rule exist, and what specific bug is it trying to prevent?
How would you implement request cancellation using AbortController inside a data-fetching useEffect?
What's the difference between a stale closure bug and a race condition bug, even though they can look similar in symptoms?
miniExercise: Build a search-as-you-type feature that fetches results on every keystroke (debounced), intentionally introduce a race condition by having a mock API randomly delay some responses, observe the bug where an older response overwrites a newer one, then fix it using a cancelled flag in the effect's cleanup.
seniorDiscussion: Your team's data table has intermittent reports from users of "the results briefly flash the right data, then revert to something wrong" when filtering quickly, but it's hard to reproduce reliably in a code review or on a fast dev machine. How do you build confidence that you've correctly diagnosed and fixed a race condition (versus a stale closure, or something else) given that both can produce similar-looking symptoms, and what would you add to your testing strategy to catch this class of bug before it reaches production again?

title: Error Boundaries, Suspense & Lazy Loading
explanation: An error boundary is a class component (there's no hook-based equivalent yet) implementing componentDidCatch/getDerivedStateFromError that catches JS errors thrown during rendering in its child tree and shows a fallback UI instead of the whole app crashing to a blank white screen - it does not catch errors in event handlers, async code, or server-side rendering. React.lazy + Suspense let you code-split a component so its bundle only loads when actually needed, showing a fallback (like a spinner) while it loads; Suspense has since expanded to also support data-fetching-driven loading states in frameworks that integrate with it (like Next.js's App Router).
whyItMatters: Without error boundaries, one unexpected error anywhere in a large component tree (a malformed API response causing a render crash, a third-party widget throwing) takes down the entire page to a blank white screen instead of just that one broken section - wrapping meaningful boundaries (a whole page, or individually around independent widgets on a dashboard) contains the blast radius. Lazy loading + Suspense is also a direct, practical lever for initial bundle size and load performance, deferring rarely-used code (an admin-only settings panel, a heavy chart library) until it's actually needed.
realExample: A dashboard wraps each independent widget (revenue chart, recent orders, usage graph) in its own error boundary, so if the revenue chart's rendering logic throws due to an unexpected null in its data, only that one widget shows a small "failed to load" fallback while the other two widgets keep working normally - and the heavy charting library itself is loaded via React.lazy so it's excluded from the initial bundle for users who never scroll to that widget.
commonMistake: Wrapping the entire app in a single top-level error boundary and calling it done - one broken widget then takes down the whole page's fallback UI instead of failing gracefully in isolation; the better pattern is multiple, more granular boundaries around independent sections so a failure in one doesn't affect unrelated parts of the page.
interviewAnswer: An error boundary is a class component that catches rendering errors in its child tree and shows a fallback instead of letting the whole app crash - important caveat being it only catches errors during rendering, not inside event handlers or async callbacks, which need their own try/catch. I like placing boundaries around independent, self-contained sections - each dashboard widget individually, for example - rather than just one at the very top, so a single broken widget degrades gracefully instead of taking the whole page down. Separately, React.lazy combined with Suspense lets me code-split a component so its JS only loads when it's actually needed, showing a fallback like a spinner in the meantime, which is a real, practical lever for reducing initial bundle size on features not every user touches.
followUps: Why don't error boundaries catch errors inside event handlers or async code, and how do you handle those instead?
Where would you place error boundaries in a dashboard with many independent widgets, and why not just one at the top?
How does Suspense for data fetching differ conceptually from Suspense for code-splitting with React.lazy?
miniExercise: Build a dashboard with three independent widget components, wrap each individually in its own error boundary, then intentionally throw an error inside just one widget's render and verify the other two continue rendering normally.
seniorDiscussion: Your dashboard's error boundaries currently just show a generic "Something went wrong" message with no way to recover without a full page reload. How would you improve this - a retry button that resets the boundary's state and attempts to re-render the failed subtree, reporting enough context to your error tracker to actually debug the root cause, and preventing an error loop if the same section keeps failing on every retry attempt?

title: Forms with React Hook Form + Zod
explanation: React Hook Form manages form state using uncontrolled inputs and refs by default (minimizing re-renders per keystroke), exposing register() to wire up inputs, handleSubmit for validated submission, and formState.errors for validation feedback. Pairing it with a Zod schema via zodResolver gives you a single source of truth for validation rules that can also be reused for typing (z.infer) and for re-validating the same data server-side, rather than maintaining separate, potentially inconsistent validation logic on the client and server.
whyItMatters: This combination is close to the industry-standard pattern for non-trivial forms in modern React/Next.js apps specifically because it solves several real problems at once: performance (uncontrolled inputs avoid re-rendering a large form on every keystroke), type safety (Zod schema-derived types), and validation-logic reuse (the same schema can validate a checkout form client-side and the API payload server-side), which matters enormously for something like a payment or account-settings form where correctness has real consequences.
realExample: A payment form uses a single Zod schema to validate amount, currency, and cardholder name; React Hook Form wires this schema in via zodResolver so submitting shows precise, field-level error messages (like "Amount must be greater than zero") without extra re-renders per keystroke across the whole form, and the exact same schema is reused server-side to validate the request payload before actually calling the payment provider, ensuring client and server can never silently disagree about what counts as valid input.
commonMistake: Duplicating validation logic separately on the client (ad hoc if-checks scattered through the component) and on the server (a completely separate validation function), which inevitably drifts out of sync over time - a shared schema (Zod) used on both ends, rather than two independently maintained validation implementations, is what actually prevents this class of bug.
interviewAnswer: React Hook Form is built around uncontrolled inputs by default, registering each field with register() and reading values via refs rather than state, which keeps re-renders minimal even on a large form - and handleSubmit runs validation before calling your submit handler, exposing field-level errors through formState.errors. Pairing it with Zod via zodResolver means the validation rules live in one schema that I can also derive the form's TypeScript type from with z.infer, and critically, reuse that exact same schema to validate the payload again on the server - so client and server validation can't silently drift apart the way two independently hand-written validation implementations eventually would.
followUps: Why does React Hook Form default to uncontrolled inputs, and when would you make a specific field controlled instead?
How would you handle a field whose validation depends on another field's value (like confirmPassword matching password)?
Why is it important to re-validate the same schema server-side, even though the client already validated it?
miniExercise: Build a signup form with email, password, and confirmPassword fields using React Hook Form and a Zod schema with a .refine() check that password and confirmPassword match, showing the error message next to the confirmPassword field specifically.
seniorDiscussion: Your checkout form's Zod schema has grown to handle several conditional validation rules (a company name is required only for business accounts, a tax ID is required only in certain countries). How do you structure a Zod schema with this kind of conditional logic cleanly (discriminated unions, .refine(), .superRefine()) without the schema becoming an unreadable tangle of special cases?

title: Data Fetching & Optimistic UI
explanation: Data fetching in React ranges from manual useEffect + fetch (imperative, requires you to hand-roll loading/error/cache/race-condition handling) to dedicated libraries like React Query/SWR/TanStack Query, which handle caching, deduplication, background refetching, and stale-data invalidation for you. Optimistic UI updates the UI immediately, assuming a mutation will succeed (before the server actually confirms it), then rolls back to the previous state and shows an error if the request ultimately fails - trading a small risk of a visible "flicker back" for a UI that feels instant rather than waiting on network latency for every action.
whyItMatters: A raw useEffect-based fetch pattern reimplements the same handful of hard problems (loading state, error state, race conditions, caching, refetch-on-window-focus) in every single component that needs data, which is exactly why most production teams adopt a dedicated data-fetching library instead. Optimistic updates specifically matter a lot for interactions users do frequently and expect to feel instant - marking a notification as read, reordering a kanban board, liking a post - where waiting for a round trip on every single action would make the app feel sluggish, but getting rollback and conflict handling wrong can show a user a misleading success state for an action that actually failed.
realExample: Marking an order as "shipped" in a fulfillment dashboard updates the UI instantly when the button is clicked (optimistic update via React Query's onMutate), so the user sees immediate feedback instead of waiting for the server round trip - but if the actual API call fails (e.g. the order was already shipped by someone else, causing a 409 conflict), the mutation's onError handler rolls the UI back to its previous state and shows a specific, actionable error message rather than leaving the UI in a falsely-successful state.
commonMistake: Implementing optimistic updates without a rollback path for the failure case, or without properly invalidating/reconciling the actual server-confirmed data afterward - this can leave the UI showing a "successful" state for an action that silently failed server-side, which is especially dangerous for anything involving money, inventory, or permissions where the user's displayed state genuinely needs to match reality.
interviewAnswer: For anything beyond the simplest fetch, I'd reach for a dedicated data-fetching library like React Query rather than hand-rolling useEffect-based fetching, mainly because it already solves caching, deduplication, background refetching, and race conditions - all things a raw useEffect fetch would otherwise reimplement, usually with subtle bugs, in every component that needs data. For frequent, expected-to-succeed actions - marking something as read, reordering a list - I like optimistic updates, where the UI changes immediately and only rolls back if the actual request fails, because it makes the app feel instant instead of waiting on network latency for every small action; the part that actually takes care is making sure there's a real rollback path and that the UI is reconciled with the server's actual confirmed state once the response comes back, especially for anything involving money or inventory where showing a false success is a real problem, not just a cosmetic one.
followUps: What specific problems does a library like React Query solve that a hand-rolled useEffect fetch doesn't?
How would you implement rollback for a failed optimistic update?
When would optimistic UI be a bad idea for a given action (e.g. a payment charge)?
